Mr. T. L. CHURCH (Toronto Northwest) moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 80, to amend the Criminal Code (motor vehicles).

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Explain.

The appalling loss of life
in this country from motor cars operated by hit and run drivers has been commented on by many supreme court and superior court judges in all of the provinces as well as by grand juries and coroners' juries. Tens of thousands of lives have been lost, and the necessity for the introduction of a -bill of this character was emphasized by Chief Justice Meredith at the London assizes last month, when His Lordship made the statement that everyone knew or should know that the provisions of the criminal code were so uncertain and inconsistent as to be quite inadequate to meet present needs in this matter. The object of this bill is to repeal the section in the criminal code relating to motor vehicles and to enact a provision w'hich will more fully meet the situation. The amendment covers reckless driving, injury to persons, racing, cut-, ting in, hit and run driving and the provision th-a-t death caused by motor cars shall be deemed to be murder. Under the code as it 
stands, murder or manslaughter may be charged where the victim dies, in the case of a hit and run driver, -but if the victim survives after injuries there is no penalty except fine under the various motor vehicles acts, and -there is no section of the -code to fit such a case. The amendments are intended to cover such cases.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.

speechtext:
A few days ago
several questions were brought forward by the hon. member for Muskoka-Ont.aiio (Mr. McGibbom) with regard to the licensing of small boats in certain waters. I observe that the hon. member is not in his seat at present, but since he appeared quite anxious to have these questions answered I would like to present a statement which I have prepared in regard to this matter.
For many years past representations have been made to this department concerning the need for rules that would effectively control the motor boat situation, to ensure that all craft operating at night should carry proper lights and that boats should not be driven at 78594-65J
excessive speeds in minor waters. Some ten years ago representations along these lines were first submitted to the department by the municipal council of Madora and Wood through Doctor McGibbon, then as now a member of the House of Commons. These representations were endorsed by the Humphrey township council and by the council of the town of Gravehhurst. Since then delegations representing the Muskoka Lakes Association, which is a particularly active body in that district, have been coming to the department urging that regulations be made and put into effect on the Muskoka lakes for the protection of the lives of those who are using these waters. These representations became so insistent that last year the department decided to enact regulations under the provisions of section 7 of .chapter 89 of the Revised Statutes of Canada, 1927, providing for the licensing and operation of small boats in certain areas. It was decided, however, that these regulations should not become effective last year. Due notice was given in the press that these regulations had beeD enacted and that it was the intention that they should become effective.
As indicating the view taken of these regulations by the Muskoka Lakes Association, the following resolution was passed at the annual meeting of that body, held on August 14, 1928:
Moved by Sir Thomas White and seconded by Mr. F. C. Gratwich that this association fully approve of the new regulations governing small boats, and that our secretary write the Department of Marine thanking the Minister of Marine, the Hon. Mr. Cardin, and the Deputy Minister of Marine, Mr. Johnston, for their kind consideration .and courtesy shown our committee who waited on them on several occasions regarding this important matter, and that our secretary in writing request that the new regulations be put in force on our lakes "as described" next spring, and also request that the Department of Marine advertise the new regulations by poster in all the post offices bordering the lakes by April 15th, and give small boat owners one month .to procure the necessary equipment before securing their licenses from the harbour traffic officer, and further that this association heartily approves the action of our executive committee in recommending to the Department of Marine Mr. W. R. Winter, our secretary, for the post of harbour traffic officer with headquarters at Port Carling. Carried unanimously.
On the 15th February last the president and secretary of the Muskoka Lakes Association visited the department and requested that an order in council be passed applying the regu-

speakeroldname: Hon. J. L. RALSTON (Minister of National Defence):
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the short time at my disposal I can only extend a brief but very sincere word of congratulation to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb), and also to the country, on the financial proposals which he has put before the house. I will also deal with some phases of the address made by the member for South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie), and in doing so I desire to pay him the compliment of having delivered an address which was marked wiith ability, but which at the same time displayed a great deal olf ingenuity and dexterity.
The hon. member is a fine advocate and he displayed a good deal of ability in selecting facts and circumstances which would best meet his purposes, and, in disregarding of omitting to make reference to any embarrassing circumstances or facts which would interfere with his arriving at the conclusion Which he sought- I will endeavour to point out one or two omissions Which he made and which, had he dealt with them, I think might have given a different impression and led to a different result in his reasoning. Take his discussion of what he called the burden of taxation. As has been done previously in this house-for want of a better argument- the hon. member disregarded entirely the fact that there had been reductions in the rates of taxation. He disregarded the fact that under this administration something like $241,000,000 in taxes had been remitted to the people of Canada, and resorted to the expedient of taking an adding machine and arriving at the total amount of revenue received during the last five years of Conservative government and comparing it with the total received during the last five years of Liberal government. He concluded with the argument that because the total of the last five years under Liberal government was $259,000,000 greater than the total of the 'last five years of Conservative rule, therefore what he calls the burden of taxation has been increased. He even went to the extent of averaging the amount of the increased burden of taxation

The Budget-Mr. Ralston
each year, and reducing that average to a per capita increase. I would point out to the hon. member that the so-called burden of taxation, which is after all t'he revenue which has been obtained from the people of this country in connection with the administration of the public services, was increased between those two five-year periods by something like 15 per cent. The hon. member cited a statement of the late Right Hon. William Ewart Gladstone that the rate of taxation meant nothing but that the burden of taxation meant everything. He knows, and the members of this house know perfectly well, that when Mr. Gladstone made that statement he referred not only to the amount but to the capability of the people to bear the burden; the burden of taxation does not mean simply the gross amount, but it refers also to the ability of the people to carry that burden. Therefore, I submit, that in this respect the hon. member omitted to mention a very important fact.
I have before me a comparison of the volume of business-after all, that is what taxation is paid upon-for those two five-year periods. These figures, which appear in the statistics of this Dominion, cover the business done in forestry, mining, construction, manufacturing, trade as indicated by employment in trading establishments, imports, exports, car loadings, shares traded in, and bank debits. The index figure representing the volume of business for the years 1919 to 1921-I am sorry I cannot give the hon. member the figures for 1918, the year he began with, because the statistics have not been made up for that year -is 93.1. I have the same figure for the last four years of Liberal rule-the hon. member referred to the last five years-from 1925 to 1928 inclusive, and it is not 93.1, as it was for the last three years of Conservative rule, but 141.8. There has therefore been an increase of 50 per cent in the volume of business and an increase of less than 15 per cent in revenue collected. That is a very salient fact which the hon. member omitted to mention. He might just as well have said because the country paid 817,000,000 more freight rates last year than was paid the year before that it can be said that there was an increase in the burden of freight rates. But there was no such thing; there was an increase in business, and business was perfectly willing to pay for the facilities to carry on and to take advantage of the prosperity which existed in this country. When my hon. friend compared the period of 1918 to 1922 with the period of 1925 to 1929, he made a comparison concerning a different Canada altogether; a Canada which
had emerged from the gloom which existed during the last five years of Conservative rule and had entered into the sunlight of prosperity under Liberal rule.
Allow me to mention another omission which my hon. friend made. It is always a good test to find out what a governing [DOT] or directing body does with the money which is paid in to or collected by that institution. The hon. member stated that during the period from 1918 to 1922 our friends the Conservatives received and spent $1,739,802,000. That is true. They received that amount and they spent it. But what more did they do? They did not balance their expenditures and I want my hon. friends to note that I have allowed them for all the expenses which are known as war and demobilization expenses.

Now my hon. friend from South Wellington selected certain figures with regard to unemployment, and he indicated that unemployment was greater now. He said that he had the employment index figures and would give them. He turned them up and gave something which I think rather astounded the house. I do not think very many people realized that there was such a figure in existence. What did he give? He gave the figures of unemployment for December 1922 as 6.4 and for December 1928 as 6.6. If he had looked at the title at the top of the table-I have no doubt that he had in his hands the Labour Gazette of February 1929, the very same book I have in my hands now-he would have seen that he was quoting from the "Percentage of Unemployment as Reported by Trades Unions", and if he had read, as he should have done, the article in which this table is inserted, he would have found that this was a report from 1,695 labour organizations with 190,000 odd members. That was not a large percentage of the number of people who are employed in the Dominion of Canada. If my hon. friend wanted to use the unemployment figures, I submit that he should not have picked out the month of December, because that is not a very good month for anybody; it is not a very good .month to select if the purpose is to indicate what the normal conditions are. He should at least have taken the average for the year. If he had done that, he would have found that the average unemploy-

The Budget-Mr. Ralston
ment figure in 1922 was 7, and in 1928, 4.5. But he could have done better than that if he had turned back a few pages in the book from which he was quoting. Then he would have found, not the unemployment figures for 1,695 labour organizations with 190,000 odd members, but the employment figures as reported by firms in Canada employing over 15 men, whether in trades unions or not, and running up to about 910,000 employees. That is the figure he would have found just a few pages back, but apparently he missed that. I am going to give the figures that appear on page 206 of that same record; they show that the employment figure in Canada in 1922 was 78.8 and in 1928, 116.6. Those are the figures which are given in the book which my hon. friend had in his hands. I wish to point out also that employment in the last six months of 1928 was at the highest point it has ever reached since these statistics have been kept.
Let me add, for the benefit of my friends from the maritime provinces, that employment in the maritime provinces for the last six months of 1928 reached the highest point it has ever reached since the record began and particularly as regards winter employment. The figures show this comparison. In November, 1927, the employment figure was
100.1,	and in November, 1928, the figure was 109.5; in December 1927 it was 99.1. and in December 1928, 108.1; in January 1928, it was
97.1,	and in January, 1929, 103.3. I have another figure even more recent, showing that in February, 1928, the employment figure was 97, and in February 1929, 104.6.

speechtext:
Where did my hon. friend

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I get them from page
206 of the Labour Gazette of February. 1929, from the returns made to the labour department by firms employing 15 men or over. t I should have liked to speak of conditions in the maritime provinces generally, with regard to agriculture, with regard to the great fishing industry which is developing there by leaps and bounds, with regard to the manufacturing industry, and with regard to lumbering. But my good friends from Pictou (Mr. Cantley) and Cumberland (Mr. Smith) have succeeded in making me feel that it is perhaps desirable, both for their information and the information of the house and of the maritime provinces, that I mention one or two matters in connection with the steel and coal industry, because that seemed to be . what particularly concerned them. They have talked in this

house for a number of sessions about what is known as the Duncan report, and they are down at the present time to one single point. I say that advisedly, because I listened carefully to my hon. friend from Cumberland to hear just exactly what his objections were. He spoke of having the Duncan report implemented in toto-that was the word he used, I listened carefully to hear in what particular respect he considered the report had not been implemented, and that one thing was with regard to steel and coal. My hon. friend from Pictou was discussing exactly the same thing. I just want to remind the house of what the exact situation is with regard to steel and coal, so that at least the facts may be put on record. There was a bonus recommended by the Andrew Rae Duncan commission, the exact terms of which recommendation were:
. We recommend that a bonus should be given in respect of steel when Canadian coal is used m its manufacture, and that the bonus should be calculated on the basis of the present drawback for every ton of coal used in such manufacture.
They recommended a bonus in respect of steel, calculated on the amount of coal which goes into its manufacture. My hon. friend says that ^ that recommendation has not yet been ^ carried out by the government, and that is the burden of his complaint. I have already pointed out to my hon. friend, and it has been emphasized on many occasions in this house, that the steel and coal industry are absolutely interwoven. I believe that no one will agree more -readily than my hon. friend from Pictou that the interests of steel and coal in the maritime provinces, and particularly in Nova Scotia, are almost inseparable and are inextricably bound up. If, for instance, assistance is given to coal, then instantly that is reflected in the price which steel has to pay for coal, and that immediately is reflected in- the question whether or not there can be successful operation of the steel plant, and whether steel at this new cost can. be sold- at a profit. On the other hand, if you have assistance- given to the steel industry, since it is located directly above the coal mines, yo-u have immediately the question whether steel may not contribute something of that assistance towards coal, whether there will not be an increased production of steel leading to a larger -consumption of coal, thereby reducing the overhead. So these two great industries are bound up, and I believe that every man in Nova Scotia and the maritime provinces generally will agree with me in that.
At the present time the coal industry in Nova Scotia is operated by a company under the control of those who own the bonds, and

The Budget-Mr. Ralston
the steel industry is in the hands of and being operated by a receiver. Last session I pointed out the necessity and the desirability of unifying these industries and of reorganizing them so that anyone who proposed that they be assisted might be able to show what earnings were necessary to make a fair return on the capitalization. There are still fourteen large companies to be dealt with. I understand that a new company has been incorporated, but that the reorganization has not yet taken place. Regarding any proposal for assistance I do feel, and I think my hon. friend will agree with me in this, that those who are vitally interested financially ought to be the best judges of how to proceed. They have to have experience of actual operating conditions in order to determine their cost of production, their markets and their competition. Now on the question of delay, it may surprise the house to know that the final coal brief, the brief on which the application is proceeding at the present time, was filed with the Tariff Advisory Board only on November 21, 1928- not two years ago as my hon. friend suggested. My hon. friend knows-I think he was present at the hearing-that that brief puts forward a request, not to the government but to the Tariff Advisory Board, that the bonus which is recommended by the Duncan report should be granted to coal. On the other hand, a brief was filed by the receiver in respect of the steel company, and almost its very first words are a reference to this same thing, namely, the bonus recommended by the Duncan report. It does not ask for a bonus for steel in so many words, but the reference is there, and it was indicated to the tariff board that the steel people considered they should be paid that bonus. This means that the coal people are asking that this relief be afforded them as part of tariff relief, and it means also that the steel people are standing off and saying:	We are
going to have it in any case, and we are going to have further relief by the amendment of several items in the tariff. It is also important to note that the final steel brief was not filed until November 23, 1928.
The coal hearing went on for three or four days after November and was adjourned until January, 1929, when further hearings took place. There is no question of delay on the part of the government or the Tariff Advisory Board. The solicitor for the receiver said himself on November 27, 1928:
The brief does raise some new points, but unfortunately, with all the effort we put on it, we could not bring it before the board earlier
than we did. We fully appreciate the position you take, and the time and care involved in any investigation, relating to an industry such as this, and of course I should think it wise that that full investigation be assured.
That is the situation with regard to those two industries. Yet my hon. friend has been complaining that nothing has been done, notwithstanding the fact that those who are in the industry admit that you must have the fullest investigation, and notwithstanding the fact that the mattter of a bounty on coal or a bounty on steel is wrapped up in. the tariff, because the foundation of the claim for the bonus is that there has been a rebate of duty granted in connection with coal coming in for steel-making purposes.
Now this question of tariffs on coal and steel is not by any means a simple one. What happened before the Tariff Advisory Board on the application of the steel company for an increased duty on billets? It was opposed by no less than three big companies. The application for an increased duty on skelp was opposed by three big companies. The application for an increased duty on sheets was opposed by thirteen separate companies. The application for an increased duty on bars and rods was opposed by eleven companies. The coal application was opposed as well, as my hon. friend knows. Some hon. gentlemen in this house are connected with those opposing companies. For instance, I understand that the firm of my hon. friend from Lincoln (Mr. Ohaplin) was opposing, as they had of course a right to do, the relief which the Nova Scotia industries were trying to get. My good friend from West Hamilton (Mr. Bell) was present in his professional capacity, and what do you spppose he was doing? I would have expected my hon. friend from Pictou (Mr. Cantley) to take him in hand. My hon. friend from West Hamilton was actually propounding the heresy that there be free pig iron. To add insult to injury, the province of British Columbia was represented officially in opposition to any increase of duty on coal.

speechtext:
It rather indicates that the application is not just as simple as my hon. friends would think. As a matter of
The Budget-Mr. Ralston

fact, it aroused considerable opposition. It is of prime importance to the Dominion to have the steel and coal schedule so settled that the industry may work under stable conditions. I believe my hon. friend will agree with me that it was physically impossible to make a new steel schedule in time for this budget when the adjournment of the hearing took place on January 29. I may say that the board employed two experts, Mr. D. H. MacDougall and Mr. J. Dix Fraser, men who were not unsympathetic by any means to the Nova Scotia steel and coal industry, and I am informed that they both concurred in the view that it was physically impossible to deal with the schedule in time for the b.udget this session.
This is a summary of the position:	The
question was brought before the tariff board, and rightly so; it was brought there by the company itself; and it is equally sound policy, in the national interest to have it considered there; the briefs on which the application^ are actually being based were not filed until November 21 and November 23, and the hearings were not completed at the adjournment on January 29 of this year; coal and steel are inextricably involved and wrapped up, and any tariff relief by way of bonus to one has to be considered in connection with the other.
I am glad to say that the year's operations have been better than those in previous years. I am glad to have it reported to me that sixty thousand tons more of coal were mined during the three months of December, January and February than during the corresponding months last year, and that there were nine days' more work last January and February than a year ago. I am glad also to have it reported to me that the steel output has increased by some 18 per cent. It is also very satisfactory to know that the extensive branch line mileage this year will create an extra demand for steel. But I do not wish the house to think for one minute that either I or the people of Nova Scotia are satisfied with the position of the coal and steel industry. The prices for coal and the prices for steel are low, particularly for certain products of the steel industry. But I believe we should congratulate both the men and the management on the way in which they have conducted the industry during the past year. I am satisfied that every fair-minded man will realize that all the ramifications and complications incident to a revision of the steel and coal tariff make it imperative that there should be the fullest investigation, as counsel for the receiver himself suggested, in order that the government may intelli-
gently study the representations which have been made to the tariff board.
My friend has spoken of the steel industry as if he and his party were the only people to whom it could look for assistance. The other night he spoke of Russian coal. I think he might have been a little more frank with the house. He did not say that that coal was anthracite coal. Nor did he state that anthracite coal is not subject to duty.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I did.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I beg my hon. friend's pardon; I accept his word. Then he did not tell us that it was his party that took the duty off anthracite coal in 1887.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Consequently there is no duty on anthracite coal, and that is why it is coming in. He spoke of Russion coal displacing Canadian coal; but as a matter of fact it is displacing American anthracite. That is the policy of his party to let in anthracite free. They are also the ones who took the duty off coke for all purposes so as to permit the Americans to convert their bituminous coal into coke and bring it in here free of duty. They had the chance to renew the bonus on steel, but they did not renew it. It is just another case of doing very little when in power and a good deal of talking when out of power. They had a chance to help the industry in connection with the rebate of duty on coal used in the smelting of metals. A rebate had been granted in connection with coal used for this purpose, and in 1914 under my hon. friend's administration the word " melting " was added so that all foundries would get their coal free of duty. I do not think my hon. friends ought to claim to be entirely the friends of the coal industry in view of their record. They gave a rebate on rods used for fencing. It was good for the agricultural industry but it did not benefit the steel industry. And what do we find on the other side of the slate? On the other side we find the steel policy of this country as laid down by Mr. Fielding in 1897 whereby a bonus was granted on steel when Canadian coal was used in its production, and that gave the steel industry in the maritime provinces its first real opportunity to make headway. But my hon. friends never renewed the bonus. We find also that the Liberal party granted a substantial duty on slack coal. It was only 14 cents at first but the Liberal party increased it to 50 cents. Again, we find the Liberal party taking coal for bunker purposes from the free list and making it liable to a duty with the result that the maritime in-

The Budget-Mr. Ernst
dustry benefited to the extent of 50,000 tons last year. There have also been freight subventions. I wish I had time to give the house an idea of what has developed as a result of the granting of these subventions in the last year. Contracts were closed for waterborne coal amounting to 175,000 tons, which were moved in addition to all rail movements amounting to 50,000 tons, and there will be moved this spring another 25,000 tons. In other words, 250,000 tons have been moved under that subvention. It may be said that some of that business would have been done in any case. It is estimated that 40,000 tons would have been carried anyway, and the estimate remains that 210,000 additional tons of maritime coal have been used by reason of the subvention granted by this government. Now I would ask my hon. friends opposite to point to anything their party has done which has increased the production of Nova Scotia coal 210,000 tons in one year.
I wished to say a word generally with regard to the report to which my hon. friend has referred, but I have not much time left. As I say, he has dealt only with one particular question, steel and coal. I have not an opportunity to point out all that has been done, but I wish the house and the people of Nova Scotia to realize that this government has tried to deal fairly with that report. Harbour commissions have been appointed and money has been loaned to them; a deputy minister of fisheries has been appointed, as recommended; freight rates subventions have been granted, such as I have described; and $875,000 by way of interim payment has been paid out yearly in addition to the regular provincial subsidy. There has been at the same time a 20 per cent reduction in local and westbound freight rates. Now I want the house to understand this, that neither I nor any other man from the maritime provinces regard this as a dole, but as a right to which the maritime provinces were entitled; and my only complaint is that this was made necessary by the fact that when my hon. friends were in power, from 1911 to 1921, they were asleep at the switch so far as the maritime provinces were concerned, permitting an increase in freight rates three times on the Intercolonial railway before there was any corresponding increase on other lines. This government had therefore to come to the rescue, and that is why I say that what has been given is not a dole. The sum of over $7,000,000 has been paid out or will have been paid out this year on account of the 20 per cent reduction in freight rates. And there has been, in spite of that-

speechtext: I have known the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston) as a soldier, and I have known him as an advocate, and as I listened to him this afternoon I came to the conclusion that he had lost none of his courage as the one and none of his skill as the other, in presenting a hopless case; and I could not help wishing that he were better informed on the subject he has presented to-day than he was only a short year ago when he attempted to dabble in the fishing industry in Nova Scotia. I recollect that in the summer of 1927 there were operating off the coast of that province two trawlers of Spanish origin. They desired to go into a Nova Scotia port and transship their fish to Spain and they sought by different avenues to obtain permission. The result would, of course, have been a much greater productivity on the part of those trawlers. Well, after trying different avenues they applied to the Minister of National Defence, who took up their cause, which he pleaded with the Commissioner of Customs, requesting that the Spanish trawlers be allowed to enter a Nova Scotia port and land their catch for shipment to Spain.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
On behalf of an apparent friend of his in Halifax he asked that the trawlers be allowed to go into Halifax in order to transship their catch, and in his telegram he suggested that such a course would have no prejudicial effect on the fisheries of the Dominion. I was aware that we shipped from Nova Scotia, or had shipped in times past, salt codfish to Spain, Portugal and Italy, and I therefore took the trouble to turn up the records from which I find that in 1927 we shipped to Spain fi^h to the value of $4,357; to Portugal, $90,702, and to Italy, $855,038. I ask the minister now whether the adoption of such a policy as he advocated in his telegram would not in his opinion prejudice the industry. Let me read the telegram. It is dated Yarmouth, N.S., July 8, 1927:
R. W. Breadner,
Commissioner of Customs,
Ottawa, Ont.
James Fraser Halifax representing parties who operate two trawlers under Spanish flag advises me that operators wish to send trawlers to Halifax to transship green fish one to the other the loaded trawler returning to Spain or tranship to French vessel for Spain. They tell me that there is some regulation under which they may be liable to pay one cent per pound. Think there must be some way out of this. It
The Budget-Mr. Ernst

is represented that it does not in any way prejudicially affect fishing industry and is serious loss to port. Would appreciate your personal attention.
J. L. Ralston.
Now, seeing that we market dry codfish in Spain, I ask the Minister of National Defence whether the first effect of such a policy as he urged in that telegram would not be to cause us to lose that market, and whether, secondly, if we lost the Spanish market we should not also in due course lose the market in Portugal, which is adjacent? Furthermore, Newfoundland, which ships large quantities to Spain, must be affected likewise. And we have to lose, too, eventually, the Italian market in order that the Minister of National Defence might gratify the desire of a friend in Halifax-and apparently without his having inquired into the industry. Such a policy, I say, would represent the sacrifice of $1,000,000 worth of business to the Dominion fishing industry.

speechtext: What was the export to Spain?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The figure is $4,357. And, as hon. gentlemen know, Portgual is adjacent to Spain. The market in Portugal represents $90,702 and that in Italy $855,038. But what I am pointing out is the principle of allowing trawlers of foreign origin to come and use our ports as a basis of operations. Once you start that sort of thing with one nation you will have bo extend the privilege to others.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: It is against our law too.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Yes, certainly. Let me direct the attention of the house again to the wording of the telegram:
They tell me that there is some regulation under which they may be liable to pay one cent per pound. Think there must be some way out of this.
It seems to me this afternoon the minister was exhibiting the same attitude towards the fulfilment of the provisions of the Duncan report; he thinks there must be some way out of it. In the case of fish, the duty was imposed by his government; his government were responsible for the collection of the duty but he, as a responsible minister of the crown, thought there must be some way out.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

speechtext: No, I do not; I presume the minister knows, but I do not think it makes the slightest bit of difference who he was. The point is that the minister was trying to find a way out of the regulations imposed by his own government.

speechtext: My hon. friend intimated that it was for a friend of mine.

speechtext: I said apparently it was a friend of the minister's, but my hon. friend will have time in due course to make his explanation.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That is the point; I will not have time.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I feel quite sure that the fishermen of Nova Scotia will require quite an explanation from the Minister of National Defence.
When the minister was dealing with the recommendations of the Duncan report he referred to the bounty of 50 cents a ton on coal used in the manufacture of steel, and I could not help wondering at his attitude. In 1927 he made a speech in this house during which he gave the house to understand that he was in favour of complete implementation of the report; during the session of 1928 he made another speech on the subject and at that time proposed three conditions which should be met before the report could be implemented. One condition was that the litigation in which the industry was involved should cease; the second was a reorganization and the third a recapitalization. To-day only the litigation has been settled, but I ask the Minister of National Defence whether it is not a fact that when the Duncan commission made its report the conditions with regard to organization and capitalization were exactly the same as they are to-day? So that Sir Andrew Rae Duncan had an opportunity to take all these facts into consideration. The capitalization was exactly as it is to-day; the organization was exactly as it is to-day, and in the face of those conditions the Duncan commission recommended this bounty.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: To whom?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
To the government, for implementation.

The Budget-Mr. Ernst

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: To whom was the bounty to be paid?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: To the steel industry in the province of Nova Scotia. But my hon. friend is quibbling-

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: " I think there must be some way out of it."

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The point is that the recommendation is there, but each year the minister brings up more conditions, and it seems to me that the only condition whereby we will have the report fulfilled will be to put the minister and the government out of office.
Now, sir, I desire to go back for a few moments to the fishing industry. Last year the minister made quite a lengthy speech in this connection during which he told of all the things the government were doing for the industry and the great progress which was being made. The latest statistics available with regard to employment in the fishing industry in the province of Nova Scotia are for 1927, and I want to compare them with the figures for 1914, which is the last of the normal pre-war years. In 1914 there were 5,832 men engaged in the fishing industry in Prince Edward Island; an 1927 there were 4,136, a decrease of 1,696; in 1914 there were 29,364 men in Nova Scotia engaged in this industry; in 1927 there were 19,749, a decrease of 9,617; in New Brunswick there were 22,034 men engaged in fishing in 1914 and 12,344 in 1927, a decrease of 9,690. In other words, between 1914 and 1927 the fishing industry in the three maritime provinces lost over 21,000 men, and since this government came into office in 1922, " this government which fosters and assists the basic industries," Nova Scotia has lost 4,230 men. These men have gone to the United States, almost without exception; if you go to Gloucester you will find that a very high percentage of the captains sailing ships operating out of that port come from the southern shore of Nova Scotia. That is the condition of the fishing industry.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Is not that due somewhat to the Fordney tariff of 1922?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Undoubtedly at is partly due to that, but it seems to me that if the government would only take a lesson from their failure to meet the Fordney tariff in 1922, we will not get into any difficulties in that respect during the coming year.
Now, what have the government done for this industry? In 1927 they appointed a royal commission to inquire into the condition of the fishing industry; that commission cost the country something over
$S5,000 and brought in a report which was tabled late last session, too late to come before parliament. Since that report was tabled, however, the government have taken some steps to assist the industry. I have seen great, flaming articles telling of what the government have done. One such article appeared in a magazine called the Canadian Fisherman, telling how the government had reorganized the Department of Marine and Fisheries. In what does that reorganization consist? The government have appointed Mr. Found, who was director of fisheries, to be Deputy Minister of Fisheries; they 'have created a fisheries intelligence service and appointed as its head Mr Paisley, who was editor of a paper in the city of Sydney, * a gentleman who knew nothing about fish but who wrote the most bitter, partisan Liberal articles to appear in any newspaper in Canada. Mr. Paisley was formerly editor of the Sydney Record and now has been made head of the fisheries intelligence service. The government also boast of the changes which 'have been made in the regulations in order to assist this industry, but those changes are so minor that they cannot be mentioned on the floor of the house.
Then we are told that the government have brought in two bills this session in the interests of the fishing industry, bills 25 and 26. One of these bills provides for the further inspection of fish and the other provides that the lobster seasons be made statutory. It also contains another provision with respect to steam trawlers, one of the most innocuous paragraphs ever to be put into any statute. This paragraph provides that steam trawlers cannot operate from our ports unless they are owned in Canada; broadly speaking, that is the provision. I say to the house that this paragraph is inserted for one purpose only; it is quite innocuous except for the fact that it is placed there to save the government from their own sins. On July 20, 1920, Mr. Edwards, the Assistant Deputy Minister of Justice, was asked to define what constituted a Canadian fishing vessel, since only Canadian fishing vessels can land their fish in the p.orts of this country free of duty. Trawlers did not actually operate until 1922, although during the war they were permitted by special order in council to operate in order to supply food. In July, 1920, Mr. Edwards gave his opinion as follows:
I am of the opinion on consideration, that the words in question-
The Budget-Mr. Ernst

That is, Canadian fishing vessels.
-should be construed to mean fishing vessels owned by British subjects .... domiciled in Canada.
If that opinion is sound-and the Minister of National Defence, as a lawyer, knows that it is sound-the government have been violating the law for the past seven years in allowing these trawlers to land their fish duty free, and now they 'bring in a bill which they wave before the fishermen as 'being of great assistance to them, but which is of no assistance to anyone but the government themselves.
I suppose they also point to the tariff provisions in the present budget; those provisions, so far as they affect the fishermen, consist of four tariff items. The first item refers to rubber gaskets; the Minister of Finance, when he presented his budget with a great flourish, announced that aid was being given to the fishermen through a reduction of the duty on rubber gaskets. So far as I can find out rubber gaskets are used for only one purpose, for sealing sardine tins, and this reduction will aid only one corporation in the province of New Brunswick.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Friends of the government.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The next item is metal
swivels; these are used by a very limited class of fishermen, and I doubt if more than 100 fishermen in the three maritime provinces use them at all. The next item is needles of a class or kind not made in Canada for use in repairing fish nets, and I think that . provision might save a man one-tenth of one cent per year. The next item covers gasoline engines and their parts. Over 85 per cent of the gasoline engines used in the fishing industry of the three maritime provinces have been manufactured in those provinces. This means a direct blow by the government at the gasoline-engine factories; a direct blow by the government at an industry in the maritimes. To sum it all up, it amounts only to a benefit of two aents per man engaged in the fishing industry.
The minister referred last year to the biological station and told us of the wonderful work which was being done in developing the process of brine freezing, which was to revolutionize the fishing industry. This brinefreezing process, which is practised in a commercial way in the United States and I believe in Great Britain, is capable of doing much for the industry, but I ask the government: How does it propose to see that this benefit is passed on to the ordinary fishermen who are scattered along the thousands of

miles of our coast? As it stands at present it will be gobbled up by the corporations and the fishermen will not even get a smell of it. What is needed is a system whereby practical fishery officers would be placed in each fishing district, similar to the system practised by the provincial governments who place agricultural representatives in each agricultural district. Under such a system the practical fisherman along the coast would be helped by the work of the biological station, and until that system is adopted I can only construe the results obtained by the biological station as being intended for the benefit of the corporations, nearly all of which are favourable to the government.
There was a majority and minority recommendation in the report of the commissioners with reference to the trawler question. The majority recommendation was that the steam trawlers should be abolished; the minority recommendation was that they should be regulated. What is the attitude of the government in relation to the trawler question? Both the corporations and the fishermen have a right to know what is in store for them; they have a right to know whether they can count upon a condition of stability. This is a matter of vital importance to the fishing industry in the three maritime provinces and I ask the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston), who represents the province of Nova Scotia, what is to be the policy of the government with regard to steam trawlers? Is he, as indicated in his telegram, seeking to find some way out of this difficulty?
The recommendation was also made that a minister of fisheries be appointed. The Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) announced to the house in his own pleasant manner that the government would appoint a minister in its own good time; that it would settle upon a policy but only in its own good time. It seems to me that the policy of this government is to do things in its own good time rather than in time for the good of the country. Immediate attention is vital to this industry and it is not fair to the fishing industry of the three maritime provinces that they should be asked to wait until the political squabbles in the ranks of the government are settled. The government has men who are capable of filling this office, men who are practical fishermen. The pronouncement upon fisheries which was made last year by the Minister of National Defence it would seem to me might better have come from the lips of some practical man who understood the industry.
I have dealt with the recommendations of the report, but there are two suggestions I

The Budget-Mr. Ernst
wish to make with relation to the industry itself. If the fishing industry is to survive in the maritime provinces we must organize the fishermen cooperatively. To-day the fisherman is buying and selling retail and the middleman is getting the profit both ways.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
What do the fishermen
actually get for their fish?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I >ean not give the hon.
member the exact price, but the average income of the shore fishermen is not more than $300 per year. They should be organized cooperatively in order to eliminate the middleman and get what is coming to them. They should be given an effective voice in dealing with the government and the corporations. In 1905 the government of Nova Scotia placed an act upon the statute books which made possible an organization in eastern Nova Scotia. That legislation was brought about through the indefatigable work of Mr. Moses H. Nickerson, who has always been a great friend of the fishermen. In 1927 that act had become obsolete and it was then amended and consolidated. During the early part of last year the minister told me that this was a matter of provincial concern. I would point out to the minister that the fisheries report, which had not been tabled at that time, recommends, on page 81, that an organizer be appointed by the federal gov-vernment. The recommendation reads as follows:
_ We recommend, therefore, that the establishment of cooperative organizations of fishermen be assisted by the department as soon as possible, and that an organizer, experienced in coperative methods, be appointed and paid by the federal government for the required period to initiate and complete this work.
The fishermen of the province of Nova Scotia are looking to the government to implement that definite recommendation. As a corollary to that recommendation, it is necessary that some system of loans to>
the fishermen be devised. I am not going to make any definite suggestion or go into the details except to say that the earning power of the fisherman is so small that he can not improve his equipment. He has no capital and if he is to survive he must have improved equipment, and the only manner in which he can procure that is by aid from the government. I ask the government to take this matter into consideration and give us some action, not next year on the eve of an election but immediately, before thousands of our fishermen have gone to the United States.
I do not intend to discuss further the technical details of the fishing industry in the
maritime provinces. There are many matters upon which I could speak did time permit, I wish in the few minutes remaining at my disposal to compliment the hon. member for South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie) on the veiy able speech which he made, a speech which has the hearty endorsation of myself and I know of every member sitting on this side of the house. It is a speech with which I heartily agree, and the only thing in it to which I wish to refer particularly is his reference to the inroads being made upon our dairy industry by the importation of New Zealand butter. There are three creameries in my constituency and I know what the effect has been not only upon the creameries but upon the farmers supplying the cream to them.
I was surprised this afternoon to hear the Minister of National Defence commending the Liberal government for the raising of a duty, because year in and year out and especially at election time, he and other hon. gentlemen from Nova Scotia have advocated the principle of free trade. The Liberal organ in the province of Nova Scotia, the Halifax Chronicle, advocates it in and out of season. Furthermore, it says that the tariff is the cause of all our worries and ills in the province of Nova Scotia. It says that the tariff has ground us down under the heel of the province of Ontario; it does not say the central provinces because Quebec is a supporter of the government. It claims that our industries are disappearing and our shipping is dwindling away. It is sad to say that that is true with regard to our shipping, but the reason why our shipping is not as great in volume as it was in time past is because we failed to take advantage of the transition from wood to steel and from sail to steam. There is no doubt we have lost other industries; some of them have located in Quebec and some in Ontario. During the last election campaign the Chronicle had a big cartoon which depicted a cow feeding in the province of Nova Scotia and being milked in the province of Ontario, a sentiment which would not tend to promote Canadian unity.
Wbat are the real facts? Let us examine the situation as it stands in Nova Scotia at the present time. I am prompted to do this because the hon. member for Hants-Kings (Mr. Ilsley) started his speech the other day by standing on a pinnacle and getting a broad view. After he had been there for a while he returned to his own doorstep and turned his face to the wall. We have in the eastern end of my province the coal and steel industries. We have scattered round our coast thousands of fishermen who supply what?
The Budget-Mr. Ernst

They export to a certain, extent, but the basis of their market is the home market, the Dominion of Canada. The great proportion of our farms are mixed farms; in fact, farmers engaged in mixed farming are more numerous than any other class of the population. They are raising their products for sale largely in the markets of Nova Scotia. We have scattered all over the province little manufacturing industries, with a few large ones here and there, some of them, it is true, exporting to the whole Canadian market and even to the markets of the world, but in the main they supply the home market. I ask the Minister of National Defence:	If that free
trade which is preached by Liberal organizations in Nova Scotia came into force in our province, what would happen to the coal and steel industries? They would be snuffed out like a candle. What would happen to the other manufacturing industries? They would also be snuffed out like candles. What would happen to the farmers and the fishermen? Well, we would continue to export them. The cause of our ills is obviously not the tariff; the cause must be sought somewhere else, because if the tariff were taken away completely, Nova Scotia would not be one whit better off in relation to the other provinces. We have, as I have said, big deposits of coal in the eastern part of the province. Developments are being made to-day by scientists, designed to promote the use of that coal to generate electric energy, and I look forward to the day when we shall be generating electric energy not only as cheaply as it is produced by hydro, but cheaper. That day is rapidly approaching, and when it comes I believe the future of Nova Scotia will lie in industrialization, but we shall not get that if we continue to follow policies which are preached by hon. gentlemen opposite. We need the tariff just as much as any other province in Canada.
_ Our difficulty not being the tariff, what is it? Geography. We are situated on the extreme eastern edge of the continent, and naturally those who have products to sell in competition with the provinces in the centre have a more restricted home market than the man who is in the centre and has his market on both sides. What we need are methods to counterbalance geography, methods which the Duncan commission recommended in the form of a decrease in westbound freight rates. That alone is the solution of our difficulties within confederation. We require freight rates which will enable us to expand our markets to the west and put our people who produce in competition with those in the central provinces on a parity with them. We have to-day a 20 per cent reduction in westbound freight rates. Whether that will be enough, 
we do not know. It has been applied; the benefits are already being observed, but time alone can tell whether it will prove ample for the needs of the maritime provinces. If it does not, we shall be back here again asking that our people be placed on a parity with the people in the central provinces, not by reductions in tariff, but by freight rates, in order that the position created by geography may be counterbalanced and we shall be given an equal share in the prosperity of Canada.
I shall not detain the house longer, but it seems to me that no method is more unfair to the people of Nova Scotia than that adopted by the hon. member for Hants-Kings and other hon. gentlemen who stand on their doorsteps, and turn their faces to the wall, applying themselves to a particular locality or industry and forgetting the needs of the province as a whole. We have to start with a unit, and that unit must be the province. If we bear that in mind and also bear in mind that in approaching our problems we have to pool them with the other provinces if confederation is to last, then we shall be building for the future a structure that will stand.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising to make a few remarks on the budget, I give it as my opinion that the budget as a financial document is possibly comparatively satisfactory; but I believe it is a mistaken idea for any nation to assume that the length of its railway lines, the wealth obtained from its mines and the strength and solidarity of its commercial institutions constitute any real gauge of its prosperity. We have to take into consideration the health, happiness and prosperity of the people. About fifty per cent of the people of Canada are engaged in agricultural occupations, and it is passing strange that, in this short discussion, little or nothing has been said about the prosperity or the lack of prosperity of the farmers of this country. The Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston) in his speech made reference to the better position of the farming industry and he suggested that in some way or another this was due to the activities of the government. I should like to point out to him that students have attributed that bettering of the condition of the farming industry to the commercial pools which the farmers themselves have organized. From practically every country throughout the world commendations have come to Canada pointing out the advantages that have accrued therefrom to the wheat growers in particular, and also to those engaged in

The Budget-Mr. Kellner
dairying. I have yet to see any such commendations in respect to any government activities, and later I shall mention instances of the lack of consideration which, I think, this government has shown to those industries.
When the minister was speaking a little while ago it seemed to me rather unusual to hear him twitting the Conservatives for actually lowering the tariff when they were in power and more or less asking for commendation from the people because the Liberals had increased the duty on coal from fourteen to fifty cents. The thought that occurred to me at that moment was that in a comparatively short time we shall likely have another Dominion election and in western Canada there will be one issue only, namely, the tariff. I wonder how many of those who in the last campaign supported this government in the prairie provinces will mention the statements made by the minister this afternoon. It would go pretty hard with some hon. members whom I see across the floor sitting for prairie constituencies, to go out and ask for support because the Liberals had increased the tariff on coal and because they had refused to reduce the tariff on some other commodities.
That agriculture generally is not in a satisfactory condition is, I think, pretty well exemplified by what we learn takes place in other countries. I read recently a debate that occurred in the British house in connection, wit the depression of agriculture. The debate was introduced by the Conservatives and discussed at considerable length. Among other things, having pointed out the great depletion that had taken place in the agricultural industry, they brought in certain recommendations to the house. Chief among those was that agricultural land and buildings should be relieved of taxes; that there should be' a marking of all agricultural products, so that the consumer would know whether he was purchasing a foreign or an English article; and the further suggestion that the forces of the crown should be supplied for at least two days a week with meat raised on the island. I would particularly call the attention of the house to the fact that it does not say meat raised within the British Empire, but raised in the island, which is considerably different from the agitation we sometimes hear for inter-empire trade. When that motion was under discussion one of the labour members moved in amendment, to leave out all the words following the word "house" and to add instead thereof the following:
Realizes that the continuing decay in agriculture is a grave national concern and should he dealt with by the government without delay, 78594-66
and is of opinion that the placing of British agriculture on a sound and efficient basis so as to yield a fair return to the farmer, -with security of tenure, subject to proper use and a satisfactory standard of living to the agricultural worker, depends upon the transference ito the state of the ownership of all agricultural lands.
In other words, we have the Labour party in Great Britain coming out with the definite declaration that the only way in which agriculture can be maintained is by state ownership.
In the United States the situation is a little different. There two bills have passed the senate for the stabilization of agriculture by what is really the fixation of prices. Both bids were vetoed by the president, and now a special session is to be called to deal with agricultural problems.
One might go on and give similar illustrations of what is taking place in other countries, in France, Italy, and Germany, in particular, where they are using every method they can to bolster up agriculture. In this country, however, our government has never been very much concerned about agriculture. Our one and only method of dealing with the problems of agriculture, apparently, is to bring in more immigrants, who will settle all the troubles that we ever shall have. There was one other thing done in this country, which, however, did not do the agricultural industry in this country any good, and that was the adoption of the Australian treaty. Some other speakers have already referred to that, and I wish to say a word or two about it.
In western Canada we have always been known as predominantly Liberal, and a good many of the representatives who have been sent from the west to parliament have come down here as supporters of the Liberal party. During the last few years they have not been quite as docile as some of the other supporters of the government, and they have insisted that the government live up to its pre-election pledges and reduce the tariff. So persistent have they been that I think the Australian treaty is the answer to their demands. The government said: We will reduce the tariff, but it will be a reduction on a commodity that affects the western farmer, and we will see if we cannot choke him off in that way. Butter coming in from Australia previous to the Australian treaty carried a duty of 4 cents. The butter produced by our western farmers was largely traded for such commodities as the farm family requires, and with the returns from their butter they would provide themselves with shoes for the children and furniture for the house. It is

The Budget-Mr. Kellner

worth while considering that on these shoes which they bought with the returns from their butter they had to pay a duty of about 22j per cent, and on the furniture a duty of about 35 per cent. The odds were against the farmer before we ever had the treaty, but after the treaty they were infinitely worse. Something like 18,000,000 pounds of Australian butter comes into western Canada every year; that was the figure for 1928. I do not think anyone would seriously argue for one minute that that importation does not very seriously affect the farmers of western Canada. You could not flood the western Canadian market with that volume of butter without very seriously affecting the price. Had other countries been giving Canada an opportunity to flood their markets with butter, if we happened to have a large stock and they a small one, it would not have looked quite so bad, but there was no preferential tariff arrangement in that regard.
Australia at present has a tariff of 12 cents a pound on butter; New Zealand, 7 cents a pound or 20 per cent ad valorem, whichever is the greater; the Union of South Africa, 4 cents a pound or 25 per cent ad valorem, whichever is the greater; the United States, 12 cents a pound, and a duty of 5 cents a pound on cheese. In addition, Australia gives a bonus to her farmers of 6 cents a pound on every pound of butter exported, so, taking into consideration the Canadian duty of 1 cent a pound, the Australian farmer has still left 5 cents per pound of government money with which to help pay his freight charges on the butter he ships to Canada. It would seem that a government that wished to do justice to the farming population would hardly pass such legislation as the Australian treaty and leave the tariffs on other necessary commodities such as I have mentioned, shoes and furniture, for instance, just where they are. The effect upon the west of the importation of this Australian butter can be readily seen from the decreased production that has taken place in the prairie provinces. In 1927 there was a decreased production of butter in Manitoba of 1,250,000 pounds, as compared with the previous year; in Saskatchewan, a decrease of over 4,500,000 pounds; in Alberta, a decrease of 3,500,000 pounds. There are a good many farmers in Alberta who cannot afford to take a drop in their production to that extent. In the northern part of Alberta the land is covered with brush, and it is a slow process to bring it under cultivation. It is the practice there, until the land is brought under cultivation, to keep a herd of milch cows, which at least

supplies the necessities of the family, but under present conditions the herd of milch cows is an additional liability, and through that district you will find farmer after farmer who a few years ago used to keep half a dozen milch cows but who to day has whittled down that number to one or two.
I omitted to mention that the United States government, as indicated by its decision to call a special session of congress, realizes that agriculture in that country is in a very critical condition, and no one would argue for a moment that agriculture in Canada could be very healthy when agriculture across the line is in such a deplorable condition.
I want to say just a. word or two with regard to this immigration policy which we are so enthusiastic about, and which is supposed to save the agricultural areas of Canada. We are frequently told that Canadians are leaving the country. I have a clipping of a statement by Bishop Lloyd giving the figures for 1928 as 81,000 odd. According to his theory about the only thing we need do to settle the problem is to go over to Europe and get more immigrants. Frankly, that is tile policy which we are following to-day:
In my poor way I am trying to show just where we shall get to if that process is continued. For instance, Canada is taxing herself to send a band of immigration agents to Europe to persuade people to come here. Then our transportation lines cut their rates and bring those people over. In the meantime government officials and others have selected the best land for those immigrants, erected buildings, put up fences and brought a certain portion under cultivation. All this having been done, the immigrants are put on these ready-made farms. The farmer already here is asked to pay taxes to bring in those immigrants to compete with himself. It is manifestly unfair to expect our agriculturists to withstand such competition, and contribute a portion of the expense as I have indicated.
And what is the position from the standpoint of our workers? For instance, suppose a Canadian gets out of work in the fall of the year, he goes to a city in search of employment, as several last fall went to Edmonton. We will assume that the Canadian Pacific Railway Company wants some employees. He goes to the railway company along with two or three immigrants and asks for a job. In the meantime the city has been feeding several hundred immigrants, but they turn them over to the Canadian Pacific Company when they find that the company had promised to provide these immigrants with work for a year. The city contended that the Canadian Pacific

The Budget-Mr. Kellner
should supply board while the immigrant was without work. The company acknowledged the obligation and supplied bread and bologna. When the Canadian citizen and the immigrants approached the Canadian Pacific officials for a joib, it is certain that the company, being a good business institution, is not going to take any chance of spending money on bread and bologna, so we know who will be rejected. One of the immigrants will be taken on and the Canadian will have to walk the streets. In all probability he is a property-owner in one of our urban centres. Pretty soon the tax collector comes around and says:	Here, your taxes are due. There
being no probability of our Canadian getting a job, the only thing that is left for him to do is to turn over his property, pay his taxes, and get out. Unfortunately our answer to any protest from him is simply this: We can go over to England and the continent and bring in other immigrants to take your place. That is the answer Canada is giving to her sons to-day.
Closely associated with the assistance we are giving these immigrants to establish themselves is the policy followed by some of our commercial institutions. For instance, I have before me a letter from the International Harvester Company, headed General Letter No. 42. Let me give it to the house:
To our Dealers and Travellers:

According to that letter, it seems to me that if you had a non-British family settler in any district, and a British family settler beside him, the one would have to pay $120 for a cream separator as against $98 charged the other. It is going pretty far to ask the established farmer to pay that extra money over the price quoted to the favoured immigrant. But I hope I have not led the house to believe that cream separators are the only things marketed in this way. I have another letter from the same company, General Letter No. 65. It contains somewhat similar preliminary comments, and then proceeds to quote prices. Let me read this portion of the letter:
Prices to Settlers: On general line (except wagons, gears, trucks and sleighs) the 1926 retail cash on delivery price less 7 per cent.
On wagons, gears, trucks and sleighs, the 1926 retail cash on delivery price, less 5 per cent.
Prices f.o.b. nearest local agent's shipping point.
The letter also contains the following:
Settlers entitled to special prices: British settlers brough out by the Dominion government under the three thousand family British settler plan, delivery to be authorized and cash settlements made by the land settlement board.
The land settlement board will have full charge of this three thousand family British settler plan, and delivery and settlement will be handled under the plan formerly governing the soldier settlers.
This is the concluding paragraph:
In view of the fact that these British settlers will not be familiar with our machines, the local agent must assume full responsibility to see that all machines are properly set up and maintained in running order, and that the purchaser is fully instructed in their operation.
