June 26, 1926. The agreement is still in effect. Let me bring out this point in connection with the second letter. It is recognized that those immigrants are not very well acquainted with farm machinery. The result is the company instruct their agent to go out to the farms and set up the machine and show them how to operate it. But when the ordinary farmer buys a similar machine he is told to take it home and fix it up himself. He has to get along with it the best he can. It simply means that the Canadian farmer is paying for this extra service to the immigrant. If we were getting a higher type of farmer there might be some sense in such a policy, but everybody admits that the one we are bringing in cannot compete with the one we are losing, and will not come up to his standard for several years
1044
The Budget-Mr. Kellner

The Budget-Mr. Marcil
where he had come from and he said, eastern Canada. They gave him twenty-four hours to get out of town, with an alternative of thirty days. On the same day there were some new immigrants in the police court on the same charge and they were sent over to the railway companies to be fed. In view of the fact that the positions in Canada are practically all going to the immigrants, and will go to them so long as there is an obligation on the commercial companies, seeing that we assume that the Canadian shall look out for himself while the immigrant is a ward of ours, I wonder why in the world the Canadian would stay. What inducement has he? The logical thing for him to do is to get out if he finds himself in these circumstances. What I started to say is this: One who has had these reverses and leaves the country, crossing the line or going to some other foreign land, must have unpleasant feelings. What must be the thought that rankles in his mind about Canada? Do you think there can be any love or affection or admiration for this land, so far as he is concerned, or will he not go away more or less with a spirit of hatred and possibly with his mind fully made up that df the time ever comes he would a good deal rather see something dreadful befall the country than see her go forward?

I have listened with considerable attention to the remarks of the hon. member for Athabaska (Mr. Kellner), who has given his views in regard to certain conditions existing in the west. I am sorry I am not as familiar with that part of the country as I should like to be in order to appreciate his statements. Some of those statements were most surprising to me, but they explain to some extent why no more energy is put into the movement to induce Canadians to go and settle in the west. In the province of Quebec for some years past a very strong opinion has prevailed that we should give to the Canadian who wishes to go west the same conditions as we provide for the immigrant. The committee on agriculture last year made, I understand, the suggestion that the railway rates should be reduced to what they were some years ago for those Canadians intending to go west. I heart, no more about it, but I am glad to know that the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Motherwell), who is a friend of the farmer, will bring this matter to the attention of his colleagues. In Quebec we are still of the opinion that when a Canadian leaves that province he should be given some inducement to go west rather than to the United States. In 1870, when Manitoba was created, the cry raised by Sir George Etienne Cartier, who introduced the bill to provide for the creation of that province, [DOT]was "Go west, young man." At that time the idea was to stem the exodus from Quebec to the New England states and divert it to western Canada. Unfortunately the west was a long way off; railway communication was difficult and other troubles presented themselves in Manitoba which induced French Canadians to go to the United States. There is a large Canadian population in those states now; it has been placed at 2,000,000 people, and they are the chief operatives in the mills of those states. Latterly, however, there has been a feeling in our province that many of those people would be delighted to go west if they wore afforded the same advantages which are offered' the foreigner. We all know that the Canadian is the best settler we can have; the man who has been born and brought up in this country, descended from Canadian people for generations, is the best man we can have and every effort should be made to induce these people not only in Quebec but in the maritime provinces and Ontario as well to go west, to counter-balance whatever foreign immigration comes into the country. We all know that if trouble should arise and Canadians should be put to the test as to their loyalty, the sons of Quebec, Ontario and the maritimeg will stand firm. For that reason I think the government would be well advised to give this matter some further consideration.
It has been said that Canada is a difficult country to govern. The day this house opened I happened to run across the hon. member for South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie), who delivered1 a very nice speech this year. He delivered another very good speech on February 11, 1901, a day memorable to me; the hon. member delivered his first speech in this house that day when he moved the address in reply to the speech from the throne, and I had the honour of following him and seconding the address. That was almost twenty-nine years ago; my hon. friend delivered a very eloquent eulogy of the Liberal party and it was all I could do to follow in his footsteps in the French language. That debate was -made memorable through the fact that the member to speak immediately after me was Sir Robert Borden, then plain Mr. Robert Borden, who was making his debut sis leader of the Conservative party. In those days the rules of the house -allowed only one amendment to the budget speech, but during the last -few years we have changed our rules, and made the problem much more difficult.

The Budget-Mr. Marcil
The position occupied by Mr. Fielding at that time was really an easy one as compared to the position occupied by the present Minister of Finance, and I may say frankly that of the twenty-nine or .thirty budget speeches I have heard delivered in this house none has been more satisfactory to the country on the whole than that delivered on March 1 last. I am satisfied that any Canadian or any member of this house whose personal affairs were in a condition as satisfactory as that shown in the country's affairs by the Minister of Finance would foe entirely satisfied.
As I have said, in those days only one amendment to the budget speech was allowed; only one issue was raised, but under our present rules we may have two amendments to the budget speech, and the two amendments moved this year show the difficult position in which the minister is placed. The first amendment reads as follows:
This house regrets that the financial proposals of the government make no provision for reasonably safeguarding and protecting the interests of those "engaged in agricultural pursuits or in industrial" employment in Canada.
If that means anything at all it means an upward revision of the tariff; it means higher protection. Then this amendment was followed by the sub-amendment of the hon. member for Battle River (Mr. Spencer), which was as follows:
That the amendment be amended, by striking out all the words after "house" and substituting therefor the following:
"urges upon the government the consideration of an immediate and substantial increase of the British preference as a step towards freer trade relations between Canada and other nations."
This means a revision of the tariff downward, so here you have the Minister of Finance following the middle course between the opposition asking for a higher tariff and another group asking for a lower tariff. I was glad to hear the Minister of Finance repeat the statement made by Mr. Fielding nearly thirty years ago, that the policy of the Liberal party was a policy of protection for the masses but a policy of lower tariff. That has been our policy since 1879. When I came to this house Mr. Fielding and his colleagues, under our great leader of those days, was trying to get the country on its feet again after a trial had been given for nearly eighteen years to high tariffs under the so-called national policy. Those who remember the conditions in Canada in 1896, after Canada had had nearly eighteen years of so-called protection, know, and if they do not know they can easily ascertain by looking

up Hansard, that Canada was then at practically a standstill. Our great western country was being deserted by its settlers; our financial condition in Quebec, the maritime provinces and Ontario was far from satisfactory, and in fact everyone wanted a change. We had been over-protected; a group of millionaires had been created in Montreal in the cotton and sugar industries, the rolling mills and in the construction of railways, and the masses of the people wanted a change in order to make Canada a cheap country in which to live.
That was the policy of the Liberal party at that time, and in 1897, Mr. Fielding and his colleagues started out by saying that they would reduce the cost of living in Canada and would give a preference to British products. So the British preference was introduced, but I can still hear the wails which came from the old Conservative party; Sir Wilfrid Laurier and his colleagues were blamed for giving a preference to England while receiving nothing in return. The Conservative party fought this British preference; they criticized it from every angle; they said it was too low in some cases and too high in others and so on, but when they attained office they allowed the preference to remain as it was.
Then in 1911 the old parliament buildings rang with denunciations of the Liberal party when it was proposed to enter into a treaty with the United States providing for an exchange of natural products. At that time I had the honour of being Speaker of the house; I put the question day after day for nearly two months, but the Conservative party would not vote on the issue and there was no means by which the vote could be taken. Obstruction of all kinds was resorted to and finally we went to the country, but unfortunately in Quebec especially the people did not vote on reciprocity. They were a unit with regard to that question in Quebec; they were all in favour of it, but the fight was carried on in connection, with the navy which Sir Wilfrid Laurier had given to the country. It was adopted by the English provinces but Quebec was afraid that it was going to be an instrument by means of which young French-Canadians would be slaughtered throughout the seven seas in defence of the flag of Britain. We had to fight a double fight-a fight on reciprocity in Ontario and a fight on the navy in Quebec. The French-Canadians are a sentimental people, unduly carried away by sympathy, and the member for Labelle (Mr. Bourassa) and the late member for Jacques Cartier, Mr. Monk, who later became Minister of Public Works,

The Budget-Mr. Marcil
realized this in their denunciation of Sir Wilfrid, and twenty-nine Conservatives and Nationalists were elected in the province of Quebec. But that will probably never happen again in our generation. The province of Quebec was fooled on that occasion, and it was fooled in 1917, and since that time the Conservatives have only returned sufficient men to report the sad news to this house.
I have not the time to say all I would have liked to say, but I wish to put certain statements on Hansard so that they may be read by my constituents. The surplus of $69,782,000 is one which should be eminently satisfactory to the people of Canada. The estimated revenue of $454,942,000, an increase of $25,000,000 over 1927-28, and the estimated expenditure of $385,160,000, an increase of $22,332,000, leaves a surplus of $69,782,000. The debt of Canada has been reduced to $2,227,068,000, which means a net reduction in six years of $226,708,000, or a yearly average of about $37,700,000. In addi-. tion to this the rates of taxation in force in 1922 have been reduced and the sum of $241,000,000 has been remitted to the taxpayers. The interest charges which amounted to $133,482,113 in 1922 have been reduced to $117,142,100 as of April 1, 1929, a decrease of $16,340,013. The payment out of revenue of maturing loans is something new, and the reduction in taxation through the elimination of various taxes has amounted to $25,000,000 in a single year. I would like to know where, in the past history of Canada, anyone could find a more satisfactory statement. I know the people whom I have the honour to represent will be satisfied with that statement.
We have heard many wails and all kinds of complaints about unemployment in this country; about those who are going to the United States and who should be kept at home. I can only speak for the province of Quebec, and will cite the conditions obtaining in the city of Montreal as compared with those of ten years ago. There are nearly one million people on the island of Montreal at the present time, and it would be very hard to convince those people that this country is not prosperous. The harbour of Montreal is rapidly becoming one of the great harbours of the world; it is the first harbour in grain exportation. Last year 453,000,000 bushels of grain from all parts of western Canada and some parts of the United States were moved through this port. The development of Montreal has been very great but progress is not confined to that city. A magnificent system of highways has been constructed by the provincial government, covering the province from the west down to the Gaspe peninsula. There has been great development in the -cities of Three Rivers and Quebec and in the Lake St. John district. That district has been transformed through the construction of enormous water-powers, the largest development of the kind in the world. Great progress has been made throughout the whole province in the development of water-powers. Twenty or twenty-five years ago Quebec was looked upon as an agricultural province but it is rapidly becoming an industrial province. Considerable improvement will take place in the Gaspe district because our railways will be linked up with the Canadian National railways. That is something which should have been done twenty-five years ago, as was done in many other parts of the country and in the maritime provinces. In many ways Quebec has improved 100 per cent as compared with its condition ten years ago. There is employment for all who wish to work. Of course, there are complaints there, as there are everywhere else, but they are nothing to what they would have been had the state of affairs which existed in 1921 continued.
Let us look at the trade of Canada at the present time as compared with what it was, not ten years ago, but only last year. During the eleven months ending February, 1929, the merchandise entered for consumption amounted to $1,130,350,273, as compared with $988,501,781 for the corresponding period in the previous year; merchandise, domestic, exported, amounted to $1,248,848,500 as compared with $1,121,233,042 for the previous year. The total trade of Canada for the eleven months of 1928 amounted to S2,109,734,823 as against S2,379,198,823 for 1929, which considered in the light of an increase of $2,352,638 in foreign merchandise exported, gives an increase of $271,816,638. If this computation were figures for the twelve months it would show an increase in one year of about $300,000,000. Where can we find a reasonable or sensible man who will! be convinced that this country is not in a satisfactory condition when he is shown figures which prove that a country with a population of under 10,000,000 people has been able to increase its total trade by about $300,000,000? In one year's time we have increased our imports 'by $141,000,000 in round figures, our exports by $127,000,000 and the exports of foreign merchandise by $2,500,000. The budget showed a favourable trade balance of $154,100,000, and nothing could be more satisfactory than that.
There are many facts which have been given in the addresses of bank presidents, the addresses of presidents of railway companies, in commercial papers and other papers of the importance of the Montreal Gazette which I
The Budget-Mr. Marcil

would have liked to read, but time will not permit. In a very interesting publication of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, Agricultural and Industrial Progress in Canada, it is shown that at the present time Canada is the fifth country in the world in point of trade. In 1927 in imports the countries in order of rank were: the United Kingdom, the United States, Germany, France, Canada. With the population that we have, that is a wonderful showing. As regards exports, Canada is in the same position and in point of agricultural trade Canada is also fifth position, the countries in order of rank being: United States, United Kingdom, Germany, France and Canada, followed by British India, Japan, Italy, Argentine and the Netherlands. We have also this statement which is a remarkable one:
In visible trade balance Canada held third place in 1927, following the United States and British India, while in favourable trade balance per capita, with $15.93, Canada led the entire world.
When I was a young lad fifty years ago I made my debut on a paper which was known then as it is now as one of the leading papers in Canada, the old Montreal Gazette. I was a young reporter in those days, under Hon. Thomas White, who was subsequently member for Cardwell in the house and Minister of the Interior. I am sorry to see that my old deskmate of those days, the hon. member for Mount Royal (Mr. White) is not in the house at this time, but we hope that he will be present before the session ends. The Montreal Gazette, which is one of the most important and influential organs in Canada, publishes every year a review of the business of Canada written by men like the president of the Canadian Pacific Railway, the president of the Canadian National Railways, the president of the Canadian Bankers' Association, the president of the Bank of Montreal, the president of the Canadian Bank of Commerce and other leading Canadians. This is a nonpolitical publication called The Annual Review of the Gazette. I find on the first page of this review for 1928 the following lines from our old friend the hon. member for Mount Royal who, let it be said en passant, is the last survivor of the men who served under Sir John A. Macdonald in the house, and we all hope that he will rapidly regain his health so that he may be able to finish his term. What does he say in this review, for he is the doyen of the Conservative party in the house? He says:
Needless to say, it has been a year of prosperity. Balance sheets work out gains. A new hope has come to the maritime provinces, crops 
have been large in the western provinces, and in the middle provinces factory production and distribution have gone beyond record. Foreign trade in value and volume outstrips precedent. Tills is the sum of the year.
That is the statement of the hon. member for 'Mount Royal, so that there is not much trouble in showing whether Canada is in a prosperous condition or not. The president of the Canadian Pacific says that his railway has gone into the construction of branch lines because it has faith in the future of the country, especially in the west. I often wonder how it is that the members for Toronto are always quasi-unanimous in criticizing the policy of the Liberal party when, under the Liberal policy, a company like the Canadian Pacific Railway, which has become the greatest transportation company in the world, is able to erect a $16,000,000 hotel in the good old Conservative city of Toronto. It shows it has some faith in the future of Canada, and that conditions in Canada are not as bad as might be thought from listening to some of the statements that are made in the house.
The president of the Canadian National Railways states that he has found satisfaction and a growing feeling of optimism throughout the whole country. It is part of his business to visit every province in Canada, and after doing this 'he says that the Canadian National this year, after paying all charges except interest charges due the government, will have a surplus of $7,000,000. Those who sat here in 1921 will remember that there was a deficit of $60,000,000 on this road. That has been changed in a very short time to a surplus of $7,000,000, showing that Canada has been making wonderful progress. The Montreal Gazette that I cited a moment ago, in publishing the annual statement of the Canadian Pacific, gives certain figures which I do not want to weary the house with, and then it has this to say:
This is a remarkable achievement, having in view the fact that so much of the company's western traffic is handled upon a low rate basis. That the gross earnings are the largest in the history of the company is evidence not only of largely increased car loadings, but of extraordinary efficiency in taking care of the traffic available.
Last year was the greatest year in the history of the Canadian Pacific. That is a wonderful thing to say, and surely we are not expected to believe that Canada is not prosperous at the present time.
Let us pass on to something else. Senator McDougald, writing in the article of the progress made by the harbour of Montreal, concludes with these words:

The Budget-Mr. Marcil
With a grand total of 423,570,557 bushels received and delivered in a navigation season the duration of which does not exceed about 215 days, not far short of an average of 2,000,000 bushels of grain passed through the harbour elevators every twenty-four hours.
Mr. A. B. Phipps, president of the Canadian Bankers Association, 'has this to say:
The calendar year just closed has witnessed a volume of import and export trade without equal in the history of the country. Abounding national revenues, record wheat production, increasing railway earnings and an unusual amount of building construction as expressed in terms of cost in the larger cities, and in fact in practically all parts of the country, have marked the year. It would be strange indeed if all this 'were not reflected in banking. Without elaborate statistics, the increase in current loans by the banks, as per return of October 31st last, of $165,000,000, or 15.5 per cent over the corresponding figures of October 31st of 1027, may be taken as indicative of the general increment in volume of banking business. If more evidence were wanted, the increment of 17.8 per cent in aggregate debits to individual accounts at clearing house centres in all Canada for the three months ended October 31st last, as compared with the like for the same period in 1927, affords corroboration nothing short of proof.
The editor of the Montreal Stock Market makes this statement:
By every possible standard of measurement or basis of comparison the Montreal stock market in the year 1928 eclipsed all prior records.
Mr. W. M. Birks, president of the Canadian Chamber of Commerce, speaking on the mercantile situation of Canada in 1928, says this:
Judged by the basal factors which determine our mercantile situation, the year 1928 has been in the van of our entire economic progress. Whether it be cultivation, manufacturing or the development of our natural resources, each tells the same story these past twelve months of an abounding prosperity, which per se indicates prosperous commercial conditions. Unless there w'ere outlets for the products of the plough, the dynamo and the exploitations of nature, there could develop no commerce of proportions. Canada has found itself in the fortunate situation, however, where marketing opportunities of unusual dimensions, both at home and abroad, have absorbed the output of her farms, her factories and her harnessed and natural wealth. More than that, the sinews of commerce have shown remarkable strength. Given the volume of output in Canada and the more than ordinary intake of imported merchandise, the transportation companies and the competing distributing agencies have all made the flow of commerce betw'een our provinces and between Canada -and outside countries particularly easy and vigorous.
These are statements which cannot be challenged. Let us see what the president
* of the Canadian Manufacturers Association, Mr. L. W. Simms, says:
During the past year I have travelled from the Atlantic to the Pacific, and have made also a number of trips which included the principal industrial centres. These gave me an opportunity to discuss business conditions with manufacturers of various lines. The general impression I received was that Canada, on the whole, is making material progress, and that the improvement evident in 1927 has been continued during 1928.
There is no branch of activity, as I said a moment ago, in which greater development has taken place in recent years than in the electrical industry, and here is what Mr. D. C. Durland, president of the Canadian General Electric Company, Limited, says with regard to that industry:
The electrical industry has kept pace with the requirements of national expansion during a year in which more electrical energy has been generated and utilized than in any similar period of Canada's history. The great activity in hydro-electric development manifest during the last few years continues without abatement, and sufficient undertakings are either at present under construction or in prospect to insure substantial progress being maintained during 1929.
At the beginning of 1928 about 4,800,000 horse-power was being generated by Canadian rivers, and about 550,000 horse-power was added during the year. The total of 5,350,000 horse-power is twice that available at the end of 1923. In other words, the annual increase during the last five years has been about 25 per cent.
In view of this very rapid increase in production and demand, it is interesting to note that Canada's potential water-power resources are estimated to be not less than 43,000,000 horse-power, a portion of which is at present unavailable because of its great distance from populated centres. Research and inventive genius, however, are -at work devising means of overcoming even this handicap of distance, while electro-chemical and other industries are following electrical projects into country which has hitherto been considered as wilderness. A typical example of this trend is that of the Saguenay river development in northern Quebec, which is now generating 540,000 horse-power at Isle Maligne Station, or twice the amount consumed in the city of Toronto. Three industrial establishments in the immediate neighbourhood, far from any city, will utilize practically all this power. These vast power resources are becoming an increasingly important factor in Canada's progress.
Already this country has the second largest per capita installation in the world, with its 513 horse-power per 1,000 of population, being only exceeded by Norway. To-day $900,000,000, representing approximately $100 for every person in Canada, is invested in hydro-electrie plants.
Could there be, Mr. Speaker, a more eloquent, a more glowing description of Canada's progress up to the present time than
The Budget-Mr. Marcil

is contained in the statements which I have [DOT] just read? In the few minutes remaining at my disposal, I shall have to leave aside much that I should like to have said. Progress has been made all along the line, not only in the hydro-electric industry, but in farming, in the development of pulp mills, in the construction of railways, in construction generally. Here is what the editor of MacLean's Building Reports says:
During 1928 the estimated value of new construction reached a total never equalled previously.
And so on.
I have reluctantly to give up my task, but the task has been a pleasant one, and I must thank those who have done me the honour of listening to me without any interruption, probably because I have become, as Providence willed, one of the oldest members of the house. There are only four or five of those who were in this chamber nearly thirty years ago, but I am glad to know that I have been able to speak in language as eloquent as I used twenty-eight years ago, when I asked my people to remember that in putting their faith in the Liberal party they were putting their faith in the true party, because the policy of the Liberal party has been at all times the policy of the people, for the people, and by the people; and no matter what changes may take place, and changes will happen naturally in all countries governed by the party system, the fact remains that when the country gets in the lurch after eighteen years of protection, and after ten years of war, when bankrupt railways have been purchased and our national credit begins to fail, and the value of the Canadian dollar to dwindle, the country naturally turns its eyes to the Liberal party to save it.
At six o'clock the house took recess.
After Recess
The house resumed at eight o'clock.

Mr. Speaker during the progress of this debate a great deal has been said about the prosperity which Canada is enjoying to-day, and I have been rather amused at the attempts of hon. gentlemen opposite to show that in some unaccountable way this prosperity is attributable to the policy of the government. Five cabinet ministers and about twenty government supporters have taken part in the debate up to the present time, but not one of them h_.s pointed to any specific act of the administration which to any appreciable

degree has contributed to this prosperity. In my opinion Canada, blessed by her great natural resources and by a kindly Providence, supplemented by the skill and energy of her people, is prospering to-day in spite of the policy of the government. If the government would adopt a policy along the lines of that suggested in the amendment proposed by my hon. friend from South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie), a policy which would make provision for reasonably safeguarding and protecting the interests of those engaged in agricultural pursuits and industrial employment, I believe the country would be enjoying more prosperity and we would have greater reason for rejoicing.
I should like to take the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Motherwell) to Algoma in order that he might hear what the farmers in that section have to say about the policy of the government-a policy that permits large quantities of fresh vegetables, and fruit grown in the United States to be marketed in this country a few weeks before the Canadian crop is ready, thus giving to the competitors of our market gardeners the benefit of the high prices then prevailing; a policy that encourages the importation of New Zealand butter, with disastrous effects on our dairy industry; a policy that in the opinion of the farmers in that section of the country is very unfair to the marketing of their hay. At the present time the price of hay is a little higher on the Canadian side than it is across the line in the state of Michigan, with the result that considerable quantities of hay are being shipped from across the river to compete in our market with Canadian-grown hay, which enjoys a protection of only two dollars per ton. A few years ago this situation was reversed; the price of hay was a little higher on the American side, but the Canadian farmer was effectively blocked from participating in that market by a duty of four dollars a ton. It would be very interesting to hear wihat the farmers of Algoma have to say to the minister with respect to a policy which they feel does not give them a fair break in their own home market.
Now, sir, in his budget speech the Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) made reference to the development of trade within the empire. In that regard he spoke as follows:
It is gratifying to note the steady development of inter-empire trade. Canada, the pioneer of the British preference, looks on empire trade as the keystone of its external trade policy, and desires in every way to foster closer trading relations throughout the British commonwealth of nations.
We are all anxious to see trade with the empire increased so long as this increase is

The Budget-Mr. Simpson
developed on a fair and equitable basis; but it seems to me that the policy of the government does not lend itself to the development of that trade, but rather to the development of trade with the United States. Let me give a few figures in support of my statement. Our imports from the United States for the twelve months ending January 31, 1927, amounted to $675,518,000, as compared with our imports for the twelve months ending January 31, 1929, of $840,353,000-an increase of $164,735,000, or 25 per cent. From the United Kingdom our imports for the same two periods were respectively, $164,635,000 and $193,451,000-an increase of $28,816,000, or about 17| per cent. Our exports to the United States in the same period increased $31,769,000. while to the United Kingdom they decreased by almost ten million dollars. Or take another example. For the calendar year 1928, the increase in our total trade over 1927 amounted to $270,548,000. Of the increase in imports 90 per cent was attributable to trade with foreign countries, and only 10 per cent to trade with countries of the British Empire. Of the increase in our exports, foreign countries accounted for 65 per cent and the British Empire only 35 per cent. It must be apparent that the policy of the government, particularly with respect to our imports, is not developing trade within the empire.
The total trade of Canada during the past year has increased by a very substantial amount. In the conduct of his own business a man naturally is very much interested to see his total turnover increase; but he is infinitely more interested in his financial statement at the end of the year to see if there has been a corresponding increase in his profits or surplus account. Now, let us look at Canada's trading account from that angle. It may be stated by some hon. members that it is not fair to compare a nation's trading with that of an individual or a private company. In some respects I admit that it is not, but the comparison which I desire to make is, I think, an eminently fair one. The following figures show Canada's favourable balance of trade for the four years from 1925 to 1928 inclusive:
1925		 $392,905,000
1926		 275,597.000
1927		 151,664,000
1928		 151,812,000
These figures show that while we have been increasing the volume of our business, we have not been maintaining a corresponding increase in our favourable trade balance. 1 am sure the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Malcolm), being a keen business man,
would feel considerable alarm if in the conduct of his business, notwithstanding the fact that the aggregate sales or turnover was increasing year by year, there was not a corresponding increase in his surplus or profit account.
How do we account for this? The explanation is that the policy of this government encourages the export of our raw material in an unmanufactured state which commands the lower price, and encourages an ever increasing amount of imports of fully manufactured goods which command the higher price. Take an example. The increase in imports in 1928 over 1927 was made up of 75.5 per cent of fully manufactured products, 2.7 per cent of semi-manufactured products and only 21.8 per cent of raw material, while almost 75 per cent of the increase in exports consisted of wheat. And our imports are constantly increasing. Take the returns for the month of February 1929 and we find that the imports in that one month have increased by $11,000,000 over the imports for the corresponding month in 1928, over $6,500,000 of which consists of iron and its products; and our exports during February have decreased by $6,500,000. This shows an unfavourable balance of trade for the month of $14,782,710. Now last year our imports from the United States amounted to $840,000,000, at least 65 per cent of which consisted of manufactured goods, which would amount to $550,000,000, 75 per cent of which could be manufactured and should be manufactured in this country, representing some $400,000,000. What would it mean to Canada if we were manufacturing all these goods here? Let us ask the Minister of Trade and Commerce to answer the question. In the very excellent speech he delivered the other day he made reference to our exports of manufactured goods, speaking as follows:
I wish to point out the value of our export
of manufactured goods. The ratio of labour to the value of the goods going out of the factories of Canada is shown to be 43.8 per cent. Hon. gentlemen who know something about industry are aware that overhead represents largely labour, expenses of sales force, advertising, bookkeeping, and so forth. All the raw material originating in Canada which goes into the factory as raw material is a finished product to the industry that produces it; therefore it represents labour. A very careful estimate-and I think it is extremely conservative-shows that for every dollars' worth of manufactured products exported from this country fifty cents is spent in the Dominion on labour in gome form or other. On this basis our total of manufactured exports represents an expenditure on Canadian labour of over $300,000,000. Allowing $1,500 as the average return for the Canadian worker, it means that 200,000 workers of this Dominion are employed by virtue of our export trade
The Budget-Mr. Simpson

in semi or fully manufactured products. Accepting the ratio of one gainfully employed in every four, it means that the manufactured exports of this country provide employment for ten per cent of our total population.
Therefore, Sir, I submit that nothing this Dominion can do is of greater importance than to assist her industrialists to find outlets for their commodities in the markets of the world; this brings employment to our working men, it brings money to our shores, and it provides markets for the raw material of the Dominion, whether wheat turned into flour, or lumber turned into sash and doors.
That is the reasoning of a keen business man who, I believe, is making an honest effort to increase the export of our manufactured goods. But let us apply that same reasoning to our imports from the United States. Last year we imported 8400,000,000 worth of goods from the United States, which goods couid be manufactured in Canada. The minister says that one half of that amount represents labour, which would amount to $200,000,000. Allowing S l ,500 as the average wage which would be pa'd, this would provide employment for
130.000	additional people in Canada-more men in this country spending their wages in the products of factory and farm. It is not hard to imagine the impetus this would give to the prosperity of Canada, and if you figure five in a family for each working man it would increase the population of Canada by about
650.000	people and would solve the problems of the Minister of Immigration over night; for no policy of immigration is better than one that provides employment for the immigrant when he lands in Canada. If you can provide the immigrant with satisfactory employment at a reasonable wage, he is going to send word back to his friends and neighbours. So that instead of spending millions of dollars to induce immigrants to come to our shores you would have them rapping at your door for admission.
I want to refer now for a moment or two to the pulp and paper industry. The development of this industry since the war has been very rapid. The production of newsprint in Canada in 1913 amounted to 350,000 tons, and in 1928 this had increased to 2,381,000, over one-third of the total world production. Canada last year exported 92 per cent of her total production, valued at $129,000,000, second only to wheat, and no small factor in the favourable trade balance which the Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) was able to show. But as a result of this rapid development our pulp and paper mills find themselves equipped to turn out a greater quantity of newsprint than they can find a market for, so that many of them have machines idle while some have been closed down completely for an indefinite 
period. If time permitted I could tell some of the experiences which the men have had to endure in some of these centres, in Espanola, a purely paper town in the constituency of East Algoma, and in another in the constituency of Fort William. This means men out of work. While the premiers of the provinces have had consultations with the paper manufacturers and have done what they could to try to remedy the situation and bring about a more even distribution of production, in my opinion this government, if they would take action, could relieve the strain with very little difficulty by placing an export duty on pulpwood. Last year we shipped to the United States 82 per cent of the total production of newsprint, but in addition to that we exported to that country 1,500,000 cords of pulpwood. This wood was manufactured into newsprint in the mills of the United States, and to that extent supplied the demand which otherwise would have been supplied by Canadian mills. If by the imposition of an export duty 800,000 of the 1,500,000 cords of pulpwood could be manufactured into newsprint in Canada it would provide
650,000	tons of newsprint or about 25 per cent of our total production, and that would enable all of the mills in Canada to work to capacity. Canada would receive $30,000,000 more for the finished article than is paid for the raw wood, and in addition employment would be provided for about 5,000 additional men. While we have great pulpwood areas, Mr. Speaker, we do not want to get the idea that our timber resources are inexhaustible; we have arrived at a point of production now whereby vast areas are being stripped of timber each year. The 1,500,000 cords of pulpwood shipped to the United States last year would represent the pulpwood from an area of 360 miles square; Canada cannot go on at this rate indefinitely and still maintain a supply for her own mills. So I submit, Mr. Speaker, that the government could relieve this situation very easily if they wished to do so.
Some person will say, " What about the settler? The settler has to sell his wood, which he cuts in the winter, in order to maintain his family until he clears sufficient land for the raising of crops." I thoroughly agree with that position; the settler must be protected, but I consider that it would not be a difficult matter for the provincial government to arrange with the pulp and paper companies that the actual settler should receive a fair market price for his pulpwood. It must be borne in mind that not over 25 per cent of the pulpwood which we export is cut by actual settlers; by far the larger portion of it is

The Budget*-Mr. Simpson
cut by pulpwood farmers and by companies which have acquired large areas of timber for the purpose of cutting and exporting the pulpwood to the United States.
Now I would like to direct attention for a few moments to the iron and steel industry. In his address the other day the hon. member for Swift Current (Mr. Both well) devoted some time to this industry and quoted from the brief presented by the Algoma Steel Corporation before the tariff board, particularly with respect to the iron ore industry. He quoted as follows:
There are in Canada reserves of iron ores of excellent metallurgical quality, and large tonnages of these ores are available and contiguous to the Great Rakes water system, and therefore in a position to be cheaply conveyed to the consuming centres, which are also situated adjacent to the same water system, but all the known deposits of ores located in this district require beneficiation before they can be used in the blast furnace. The cost of beneficiation is in excess of the cost at which American lake Superior ores can be laid down at Canadian furnace docks at the present time, and therefore^ governmental assistance in the way of bounties would be required to firmly establish a Canadian iron ore industry.
He quoted further from the brief, as follows:
.... until increased mining costs in the American iron ore fields force the price of ore well beyond present levels, we will be unable to proceed with the development of this important future source of supply.
His comment was as follows:
That was the statement made before the tariff board. If the situation in Canada is such that it is going to cost us considerably more to use our own ore and coal in order to manufacture iron and steel, s.urely at this time it is good business for us to get our iron and steel from some other place.
The statement he read from this brief is substantially correct with respect to the iron ore situation in this counry. We have large quantities of iron ore in different sections of. Canada; in northern Ontario particularly there are large deposits of siderite and magnetite ores, but none of this ore is suitable for blast furnace use in its natural state. It has to be treated; the sulphur, phosphorus and other impurities must be removed and the iron content raised before the ore is suitable for blast furnace use. This costs money, and as a result not a ton of iron ore is being mined in Canada to-day for use in Canadian blast furnaces; the ore is secured from the iron mines of the United States or Newfoundland. However, I contend, Mr. Speaker, and I am backed up in this contention by the commission appointed by the Ontario government some years ago to investigate the iron ore situation, that it is not in the national interest for Canada to be dependent upon
another country for the raw material of such a great basic industry as that of iron and steel. This commission, having made an exhaustive study of the whole situation, recommended that a bounty should be paid in order to assist in meeting the cost of the treatment of this ore, one-half of the bounty to be paid by the province and the other half by the Dominion. So far as the province of Ontario is concerned, two or three years ago they provided for the payment of their share of the bounty, but although my hon. friend from Fort William (Mr. Manion) and myself have endeavoured to impress upon this government the necessity of providing their share of the bounty, up to the present time they have not seen their way clear to do so.
Just here I would like to refer to the mining of ore from the Helen mine, when it was in operation, in order to give an idea of what this would mean to Canada. This was a mine at Michipicoten which was operated for a few years, during which time a little more ore was taken from it than was imported into Canada last year, and I will give the actual result of the operation of that mine during that length of time. The company paid in wages $1,820,000. in freight SI,642,000 and for supplies $1,020,000, or a total of $4,482,000, and it is estimated that at least $700,000 of that total was for farm produce. We must bear in mind that the cost of mining ore is almost entirely in wages and freight rates, and I contend that it would be very much in the interests of Canada to keep that money circulating in our own country instead of sending it to the United States.
Some people are opposed to the principle of bounties, and in that connection I would like to quote what Mr. Fielding had to say. As the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston) stated this afternoon, we are indebted to Right Hon. W. S. Fielding for providing a bounty for the iron and steel industry about 1900, which bounty was paid for about ten years. Referring to this fact, Mr. Fielding said:
In tliis connection,, I would like to invite the attention of the house to the question of what these bounties have accomplished. I know that with some excellent citizens of Canada the idea of bounties is not popular. More than once I have met people of the very best class who shake their heads over the idea. I think, however, that it can be clearly shown that the treasury of Canada has not lost one dollar from the payment of bounties. The iron and steel industries which have been established in the country have undoubtedly had a great effect in the development of the trade in Canada. Just how far the influence of a steel industry is felt may be a matter of debate. I have no doubt that honourable gentlemen have found many cases where business has been influenced favourably a long distance
The Budget-Mr. Simpson

from the location of an iron and steel plant; I have found such cases myself; and it must be remembered that in all the principal trade centres of Canada vast quantities of goods have been purchased and sold to these steel ports, as I may describe them.
He goes on to show that the 'Collection of customs duties at ports where steel industries were established increased materially as a result of the increased business carried on after the bounties had been paid. He gives a comparison of the ten-year period before the bounties were paid and the ten-year period during which they were paid, which shows that the customs duties collected in the first period amounted to $7,708,566.69 and in the second period, $16,710,211.72. The collections at the port of Sault Ste. Marie increased by almost $1,000,000 per year for the ten-year period subsequent to the payment of bounties. From three to five million dollars was paid annually in wages, and large sums were also paid to our railways as a result of the operations of the steel mills in that city. Since the war the steel industry in Canada has had to contend with very unfair competition in its own market from the large steel industries in other countries, especially the United States. Last year I presented to this house as clearly and as frankly as I could the reasons why we considered this competition was not in the interests of Canada. I offered a concrete suggestion as to how it could and should be remedied. Time will not permit me to repeat this argument to-night, but I will read an extract from the brief submitted by the Al-goma Steel Corporation to the Advisory Board on Tariff and Taxation, which shows that our steel industry was operating at less than fifty per cent of capacity, although equipped to manufacture practically all the steel which was imported, with the exception of some of the larger shapes of structural steel. In part, the brief reads as follows:
From these figures it will be noted that during these seven years (1921 to 1928) our steel-making capacity has been employed only to the extent of 39 per cent of rated capacity, and that in only one year did we exceed 50 per cent, vizr the fiscal year ended June last. The increase in that year was due entirely to the increased demand for standard rails and fastenings.
While our mills -were operating at less than fifty per cent of their capacity, we find importations increasing at an alarming rate. Under the heading Iron and Its Products we find the following imports:
1925		 $134,684,441
1926		 181,196,800
1927		 229,429,485
Twelve months ending
January 31, 1929.. ..	330,953,152

There is an increase of over $100,000,000 since March 31, 1927, and of 150 per cent in a period of less than four years. What does this mean to the men engaged in this industry? The following appears in the brief of the Algoma Steel Corporation:
The salaries and wages paid during this period (1921	to 1928) amounted to
$22,501,555.65, or an average of $3,214,507.95 per annum. Assuming full employment for our steel-making capacity, the additional wages paid within our own plant would amount to upwards of $2,000,000 per annum.
Is it any wonder, Mr. Speaker, that those interested in building up the steel industry of this country, and those dependent upon that industry for employment, are asking for a policy which will give them a fair chance in their own market? It is not necessary for me to argue the question further. The government, and particularly the Minister of Finance, is thoroughly familiar with the whole situation. What we want is action. This matter has been before the government for three years; it was one of the first matters placed before the tariff advisory board for their consideration. What I desire to ask, and what the people whom I represent desire, to know, is why no provision has been made in the budget of this year to relieve the situation. The government cannot say that there has not been sufficient time in which to thoroughly investigate the matter. I ask the minister in all sincerity to have the courage to adopt a real Canadian policy, one which will enable us to carry on the manufacture of iron and steel within our own country and provide more steady employment for the men engaged in that industry.

speakeroldname: Mr. D. J. COWAN (Port Arthur-Thunder Bay):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is customary to congratulate the member who speaks before you and on this occasion I have very great pleasure in conveying my congratulations to one of my " fellow citizens who is also a fellow Conservative. The sentiments which he has expressed are those which are dear to my heart. The fact that there are to be no speakers from the other side of the house this evening may be an indication that we have finally tamed them into submission, or perhaps they have realized the hopelessness of answering the arguments which have been developed from this side of the house. I propose to address myself to what is not included in the budget proposals.
By the budget proposals introduced by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) the government has invited the house to display a trustfulness, not to say credulity which might well tax the faith of the most docile and best dis-

The Budget-Mr. Cowan
ciplined majority. One would have thought that the Liberal lions, particularly from the west, would have demanded a bigger banquet.
In view of the dangerous situation which may arise after the summoning of the congress of the United States, it seems to be the government's policy to mark time with regard to tariff changes; apparently it is the desire of the government to wait and see. The action of the government in deciding to postpone the tariff changes has caused serious and widespread disappointment. It means that all the work of the tariff advisory board during the past year has been swept temporarily into the dust-bin. Many great industrial corporations have spent thousands of dollars in preparing their case and in having it heard before that board. The steel, coal, electric-stove and foundry companies, as well as those requesting a revision and aid in the coal, steel and iron industries have all gone to the greatest trouble to collect their information. The failure of the Finance department to carry out any of the recommendations of the tariff advisory board, or to submit to the House of Commons any such recommendations or findings as have been made by that board, will be found to reflect seriously upon the prestige of the board. Unless action follows as a result of these hearings, in future the industrial companies will decline to go to the trouble and expense of preparing their case for presentation to the board, especially in view of the fact that during the last two years the board has given every indication of deciding these applications on purely political grounds. There has been at all times a juggling and shifting between the tariff board and the Department of Finance until the public and the applicants before that board do not know upon which they should place reliance, or upon whom the blame should be placed for delays or postponements. This deception is parallel to that which was practised upon the patriarch of old Isaac; when he desired to confer a blessing upon his son, through the deception of his wife another son was substituted until the blind old man exclaimed: "The voice is Jacob's voice, but the hands are the hands of Esau."
The Postmaster General (Mr. Veniot) in his speech the other day had some remarks to make in regard to the action of the acting leader of the opposition, the hon. member for South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie). I am not entering upon a defence of the action of the hon. member for South Wellington. He needs no defence at my hands, nor at the hands of anyone else, for his presentation of the arguments against the budget was one of the high
lights of the session. As we on this side of the house watched the countenances of hon. members opposite, we could not help feeling that many of them could only be said to be envious of the courage of the man who could follow his convictions. It was apparent to any observer that his amazing eloquence and convincing logic had almost forced them to exclaim as did that old and troubled Roman governor years ago: "Almost thou persuadest me to be a Christian." The present administration have not that forward look; they are looking at the past instead of at the future, and I propose during the few minutes at my disposal to discuss some of the subjects which I submit, in all fairness, should have been included in the budget.
The first matter I wish to discuss is that of highways. The subject of aid to international highways or a trans-Canada highway was introduced into the house by the hon. member for Athabaska (Mr. Kellner). The situation in Ontario, and particularly in the district of Port Arthur and Fort William, is one that calls for special treatment. In 1S67 confederation became .possible by the building of the trans-Canada railway. The unity of Canada may be made more permanent by the completion of a trans-Canada highway for motor cars. The motor car of to-day is a universal means of transportation of freight and passengers, and the construction of a trans-Canada highway is capable of hastening the unity of Canada, of bringing the east and the west together, of stimulating the development of Canada in a fuller measure than is possible by any other means. The motor car demands an all-weather surface highway, much as the railway train requires steels rails. Its degree of efficiency in solving the problem of transportation is in large measure disappointing owing to the absence of proper highways. All our previously accepted ideas of highways and their use must be revised in the light of the usefulness of the modern .motor car and its amazing efficiency. Experts in construction of highways admit that all-weather motor highways are of material importance, and that the greater initial expense in their construction is amply justified. Highways are a matter not only of local interest but of national importance. The whole nation gets the benefit of them. From a national point of view highways are necessary for postal service, for trade and commerce, and for the general welfare of our citizens. It has now been recognized in the transportation world 'that motor highways, meaning thereby all-weather roads, rival even the railways in the extent of their operations and the service which they render to the
The Budget-Mr. Cowan

public. We all know that in Canada railways were early recognized as of national importance, and to supply the necessary encouragement to bring them into existence the people of Canada gave large and valuable land grants to the promoters and guaranteed their bonds as well. The people of Canada must do the same thing, but in a different manner, for the national highways. The highways when built remain the property of the public; they do not become the property of private corporations. It is not possible, therefore, to induce their development by giving land grants. It must be done by way of cash subsidies. In 1919 the Dominion government, in cooperation with the provinces, arranged a plan whereby the sum of $20,000,000 was set aside by the Dominion government for main highway construction in Canada, out of which under the arrangement arrived at, the Dominion government paid to the provinces 40 per cent of the cost of contruction, the routes for the various highways being worked out in conjunction with the provinces. I think the proposed construction of a trans-Canada highway embodies a sound national policy and should be accepted as outside and above party politics.
The federal government of the United States has, since 1917, expended more than $650,000,000 among the various states of the union to stimulate and assist them in building their main system of highways. In proportion to the effort that has been made by the United States, $20,000,000 from the federal treasury in ten years is a very small amount. If Canada were making to-day the same effort as the United States, the amount spent on highways by the federal government would amount to $60,000,000. The advantage which would accrue to Canada as a whole by the construction of a trans-Canada highway cannot be measured in dollars and cents. It is estimated that citizens of the United States spent in Canada last year hundreds of millions of dollars. Tourists will not travel in Canada unless good motor roads are provided. There are 20,000,000 motor vehicles being used in the United States of America. The people there believe in using their cars for both pleasure and business; they have built the most wonderful highways throughout the length and breadth of their immense country, and in order to attract them to our northern country we must have all-weather motor highways throughout the Dominion. There is as yet not one transcontinental highway across Canada. We realize in the cities of Port Arthur and Fort William and in the surrounding districts the advantages of having a highway between Duluth and Port Arthur.

The value in dollars and cents to the merchants, hotels and business people of those communities of the traffic coming over this route is of transcendent importance. The provincial government should not be obliged to pay the whole cost of the construction of the remainder of the road extending east from Port Arthur to Sault Ste. Marie. This is a work of national and not provincial importance, and a portion of the expense should be borne by the national treasury. I suggest in this connection one other thought; the western provinces, including the district which I represent, have a large mileage and a sparse population. The contemplated highway is a provincial asset and not merely a local improvement. Federal aid should, therefore, be granted to the provinces in proportion to the mileage to be constructed rather than on the basis of population. This highway policy which has been adopted in-the United States has worked out very successfully there and I urge upon the government of the day the advantage of adopting the same policy in our own country.
A year ago, speaking in the budget debate, I advocated the policy of the extension of our air mail routes. This method of the transportation of mail has been tried by the Post Office Department to some extent in eastern Canada. I would urge the government.to establish an air mail service from Montreal and Toronto to western Canada. I need not dilate on the necessity of rapid transportation of mail. I think the system has got beyond the stage of an experiment. Even now it is certain that a great saving in time will be achieved, and that, after all, is the primary end of air mail service. To-day the post office is a vital and indispensable part of organized daily life, and especially .of business and commerce. No possible method of making a more efficient and serviceable handling of mail can be ignored by the postal authorities. It is but a natural development in the evolution of mail delivery that airplanes should be adopted wherever possible. It requires 48 hours for mail by the present mode of transportation to pass from Port Arthur to Montreal, and 60 hours from Winnipeg to Montreal. This by a proper service could be cut down to 10 and 13 hours respectively. I understand that the advantages of the service which has been put on between Rimouski and Montreal have received favourable comment. In the United States the air mail service was put into effect on the 15th of May, 1918. It has met with a gradual response from the mailing public, and has now reached the stage where it has be-

The Budget-Mr. Cowan
come a daily factor in the business life of the communities throughout that country. Prior to February 15th, 1926, the air mail service in the United States was operated by the Post Office Department. On that date, the air mail service under contract between the Post Office Department and private individuals or corporations was established, and on September 1, 1927, the government relinquished its operation of the air mail service, and now all mailing routes are under contract. I think it is taken for granted that the service provided by airplanes would be more expensive to the department. An increase in the air mail postage rate would help to bear a portion of the extra expense thus incurred. In the United States they have adopted a rate of 10 cents per half ounce, as compared to a rate of 2 cents per ounce for ordinary first-class mail. This increase in the rate would create a fund to offset the increase in the cost to the department for transportation of mail by aircraft. Naturally every city could not have delivery of mail by aircraft, but means could be found of distribution from the larger centres to the smaller communities.
Now I turn to the question of the waterways. One of the questions which had been discussed a great deal in the press, by engineering societies, and by the people generally, is that of a highway to the sea. Should there be a deep water canal connecting the Great lakes with the Atlantic, and what should be our relation with the United States in connection therewith?
We must keep in mind the fact that the United States is insisting upon a seaway by way of the Great lakes and the St. Lawrence, and if Canada does not cooperate, the question of an alternative route through the United States must be considered. This is one of the important questions that has arisen in Canada during the first quarter of the twentieth century, and upon this important question no lead or direction has been given by the Prime Minister or the government of the day. The policy of the government seems to be one of shuffling and evasion. It is to be observed that no communication has passed from Canada to the United States in regard thereto since April 4, 1928, that no advance has been made in the matter of determining the respective jurisdictions of the provinces and the federal authorities and that at least another year will pass away before the government takes any step to reconcile the interests of the provinces and the Dominion.
If any conclusion can be drawn from the attitude and actions of the government, it
is that the water-power privileges are the dominant factor and the chief interest underlying the waterways project. This may be of interest to eastern Ontario and a portion of Quebec, but it does not take into account the long view of the interest of the rest of Canada in the canalization of the St. Lawrence river. This is certainly a work for the general advantage of Canada, and the opinion has been freely expressed that it would have been better business to have withheld action on the water-power franchises until the whole scheme had been worked out and a settled policy determined upon as regards both the water-power development and the construction of the canal. I think the time is opportune for the government to give a lead to the discussion on this subject, and that the attitude of the government should be presented to the house and to the public. According to the press reports, a great body of public opinion in the United States views with alarm the franchise proposed to be given to the Beauharnois Power and Canal Company. It is easier to retain than to regain privileges and franchises, and it is the more remarkable in view of the fact that the St. Lawrence advisory commission recommended that the cost of the construction of the canal should be paid out of the sale or earnings of the power franchises. It would appear that the day is past when the cost of the canal is to be borne in the manner suggested by the advisory board. I think the Prime Minister owes it to the house and to the country to state in unequivocal terms the attitude of himself and his government towards this enterprise, so that we shall know the position we are in, and the course he proposes to take.
I intend for a few moments to elaborate on the argument which has just been presented by my hon. friend from West Algoma (Mr. Simpson) with regard to the iron ore situation. The importance of the iron and steel industry in Canada warrants exceptional measures being taken to make that industry as far as possible self-sustaining in regard to its supply of raw material. For* the last calendar year, and for several years prior thereto, not a ton of iron ore has been mined in Canada or used by Canadian furnaces. This is a condition that should not be allowed to continue.
The great area of northern Quebec, northern Ontario and Manitoba, known as the precambrian shield, is the most highly mineralized area in the world. Geologists tell us that in that geological formation is found all the great mines that are in existence to-day. Eighty-five per cent of the pre-
The Budget-Mr. Cowan

Cambrian formation is in Canada and the remainder is in the United States. The 15 per cent in the United States we find in the great Mesaba range, upon which to-day the prosperity of the United States depends in regard to steel and iron products. Our balance of trade is adversely affected to the extent of over $300,000,000 by the importation of American ores during a period of twelve months.
Under the system of bounties on certain mineral products, there was paid out of the federal treasury up until the year 1911 the sum of $17,000,000. At that time a great number of blast furnaces were established' in Canada, at Hamilton, Port Colborne, Midland, Parry Sound, Deseronto, Ojibway, Port Arthur and Sault Ste. Marie, but many of these have ceased to operate as a result of the discontinuance of the bounty provided.
The advantages to be gained by the use of our own ore are apparent to anyone who has given any thought to the subject. Sufficient investigation has been made to demonstrate that there are iron ores in Canada in sufficient tonnage that could be made available immediately by some preliminary treatment. I urge that the federal Department of Mines should conduct experiments to demonstrate an efficient method of bene-ficiating our low grade iron ores, and assistance by means of a bounty would encourage the installation of extensive plants and permit Canadian furnaces to utilize Canadian ore. Researches have been conducted in the state of Minnesota to demonstrate the most economical metallurgical methods of bringing our low grade magnetites up to merchantable grades. The United States Bureau of Mines at Duluth have been experimenting on ores similar to our own, but of much lower grade, giving from 20 to 27 per cent iron content. I think the department could well make use of experiments so conducted, as they have extended over a period of years. Extensive areas have been explored in many parts of Canada, and I have no reason to doubt that concentrates of merchantable ores will be found in these ranges. This is particularly true of northern Ontario, which on more than one occasion has been referred to as the breaking point between eastern and western Canada.
The development of the iron ore industry would increase the revenue of our railways. It is estimated that at least 65 per cent of the tonnage of the railways in the United States is derived from the products of the (nines. It would help to solve the question of providing tonnage and earning power for

the Canadian National Railways. It would stimulate the development of all our mining activities, and the increment in the revenues of Canada that the proposed bounty would require would amount to only a very small tax. I would urge the Minister of Finance to take advantage of the opportunity of granting needed assistance to this industry, particularly in view of the fact that the Ontario government in 1924 passed what is known as the Iron Ore Bounty Act, for the very purpose of assisting this industry. It is to be noted in this connection that the treasury would be assuming no responsibility if no iron ore was produced). I suggest it is worthy of a trial to ascertain whether the producers with the aid of a bounty could make a success of the enterprise or not. The advantages are numerous, and the disadvantages are not evident. The Minister of Finance should, therefore, take advantage of the Ontario act, and the Dominion should contribute a sum sufficient to put this enterprise upon a satisfactory basis.
It is a striking commentary on Canadian industry that the number of men employed in blast furnaces in 1913 was 1,589 and that in 1925 the number had been reduced to 656 and is still less at this date. There are now only three furnaces in operation in Canada, and their total output is only 21 per cent of the total capacity of such furnaces.
Iron ore, coal and steel are the three main roots that give life to and support the trunk of the iron trades tree. No matter how wide-spreading and fruitful its branches, if this tree has its roots outside of Canada it is not a Canadian possession. It is time now to establish, in cooperation with the province of Ontario, this industry on a permanent and successful commercial basis. The time to begin is now, in order that it may be fairly established within the next ten years.
There are many iron ore deposits in northern Ontario that would be developed if this legislation should receive approval, and I know of no legislation of a constructive character that would be of greater advantage to Canada as a whole.

' Mr. Speaker, in rising to say a few words in connection with the budget, it is not my intention to enter upon any discussion of the financial standing of the Dominion of Canada. This question has already been dealt with, and will probably be touched upon later. 1 may say, however, that the man by the roadside oannot help but be of the opinion that a surplus of practically 170,000,000 is a fairly satisfactory condition so far as the finances of the Dominion are concerned.
There are things in the budget which I like and things which I do not like. I am very glad that this year the income tax has been left untouched. I am pleased also that the sales tax has been reduced, because this is a tax which affects practically the whole consuming public. We have heard a great deal about the prosperity of Canada, and perhaps if we measured that prosperity on the basis upon which it has been measured in this house we might believe that our present prosperity has never been exceeded. But I am of the opinion that this prosperity has not been equally distributed; the primary producer has not been getting his share of it. I do not propose to pick out any extreme cases to illustrate this point. The reason why the primary producer is not enjoying to the extent he is entitled the prosperity that exists at present is because in every case he has to take what is left of the price that is paid for the commodity he has to sell. The transportation people get their share first; the distributing organizations get theirs next, and the remainder goes to the primary producer. It costs just as much to distribute grain whether it grades the highest or whether it comes down six or eight grades below the top. Last year, until a very short time before the binders were put into the fields in western Canada, we were promised an abnormal crop. Climatic conditions, however, intervened during the last few weeks of its development, with the result that a large percentage of the grain in western Canada fell into very low grades. That is, there was passing through the inspection department in Winnipeg more grain grading No. 5, No. 6, and feed, than any other grade. A few days ago I picked up a paper which gave the shippings to the head of the lakes, and it was shown that for the week ending March 8 more grain grading No. 5 was shipped than any other grade. This, according to the figures that were given, was worth about twenty-five cents a bushel less than No. 1 northern, or the top grade of wheat. The same conditions applied to oats and barley; the

The transportation company received 45 cents per bushel for carrying the potatoes from the maritimes to Winnipeg, and I am told by some of my maritime friends that the farmers were receiving around 20 cents a bushel.
